Show results from: Clear search input Search for result Max Clear search input Search for result Article HPV explained for young people: questions, myths and facts that matter Drawing on young people's voices, we explore what HPV is, what the evidence tells us about vaccination, and why who communicates about prevention – and how – makes a difference. Valeria Dumitriu-Furculiță UNICEF/2026/Moldova Română English 16 October 2026 Drawing on young people's voices, we explore what HPV is, what the evidence tells us about vaccination, and why who communicates about prevention – and how – makes a difference. This year, approximately 160 adolescents and young people volunteering with Youth Klinic Moldova gathered with their coordinators for the 11th edition of the Youth Klinic Moldova Summer School for Volunteers and Volunteer Coordinators. The participants are part of a national volunteer network established across the country's 40 youth-friendly health centres. Over five days, they strengthened their knowledge and skills to carry out peer-to-peer information and education activities, focusing on two key topics: preventing gender-based violence and human papillomavirus (HPV) infection. During the HPV sessions, volunteers explored how the virus spreads, the health conditions it can cause, vaccination and screening, as well as the myths and misinformation circulating, including online. Through brainstorming, role-playing, myth-busting exercises, and guided discussions, they practised not only what information to share but also how to have these conversations with other adolescents. For some, the topic was almost entirely new. "To be honest, it was only at this camp that I learned about HPV. Before that, I didn't know about the virus or how common it is," says Victoria, a 15-year-old Youth Klinic volunteer from Anenii Noi. Victoria was not the only participant to leave Holercani with new questions, answers and ideas to share with others. Other young people arrived with specific questions or recognised myths they had already heard at home, at school or online. But what should adolescents actually know about HPV? HPV is extremely common. Most of the time, we don't even know we have it. HPV is not a single virus, but a family of approximately 200 viruses. It is one of the most common sexually transmitted infections. According to the World Health Organization (WHO), almost everyone who is sexually active will acquire HPV at some point in their lives, usually without experiencing any symptoms. In approximately 90 per cent of cases, the body clears or controls the infection without medical intervention. UNICEF/2026/Moldova "Most HPV infections cause no symptoms and are cleared by the body. The risk arises when an infection with a high-risk HPV type persists and gradually causes changes in cells. This process usually develops slowly, which means there is time to intervene. Vaccination helps prevent infection with the HPV types covered by the vaccine, while screening can detect precancerous lesions before they develop into cancer," explains Angela Capcelea, Health Specialist at UNICEF Moldova. HPV is the cause of cervical cancer and is also associated with cancers of the vulva, vagina, penis, anus, mouth and throat. Globally, approximately 660,000 women were diagnosed with cervical cancer in 2022, and around 350,000 died from the disease. In the Republic of Moldova, approximately 150 women die from cervical cancer each year, while around 300 are diagnosed with the disease. HPV is not just a girls' issue One of the important messages discussed by Youth Klinic volunteers was that HPV affects both boys and girls. "After the HPV session, I took away three important messages: both girls and boys can get HPV; the HPV vaccine does not cause infertility; and HPV is a serious issue that needs to be addressed responsibly. Even though people don't talk about it very much, we need to start paying more attention to it," says Dumitrița, 16, from Orhei district. UNICEF/2026/Moldova/DanBragoi Because HPV is most commonly discussed in connection with cervical cancer, it can create the impression that the virus is only a concern for girls and women. In reality, HPV can cause health conditions and cancers that affect both sexes. UNICEF/2026/Moldova UNICEF/2026/Moldova The HPV vaccine and fertility: What does the evidence say? Of all the myths discussed by the young participants, one came up particularly often: the belief that HPV vaccination could affect fertility. Ludmila, 17, from Leova, says she frequently encounters this misconception among both young people and adults. "People often listen to other people's opinions without checking whether the information is accurate. That's why it's important to speak with confidence and present evidence from reliable sources," she adds. Vlad, 15, who has been a Youth Klinic volunteer in Florești for more than two years, says he has also encountered concerns that a girl who receives the vaccine may no longer be able to have children. The available scientific evidence does not support this claim. UNICEF/2026/Moldova "The HPV vaccine does not contain a live virus and cannot cause HPV infection. Evidence gathered following hundreds of millions of doses administered worldwide confirms a strong safety profile. The most common side effects are similar to those associated with other vaccines, such as pain at the injection site, a mild fever or temporary discomfort. Available evidence does not indicate that HPV vaccination causes infertility," adds Angela Capcelea, Health Specialist at UNICEF Moldova. Moreover, preventing cervical cancer can itself help protect reproductive health, as treatment for severe precancerous lesions or cancer may have significant consequences for a woman's health. Autism, "genetic mutations" and other myths: Where do they come from, and why do they persist? Some of the questions young people encounter are more unexpected. "During a workshop, a child came up to me and asked whether getting vaccinated could cause genetic mutations," recalls Dumitrița. For her, questions like these demonstrate how important it is for adolescents to have access to accurate, easy-to-understand explanations. Victoria says she has also heard claims that vaccines can cause autism. On 3 September 2026, WHO published a new systematic review of studies conducted between 2010 and August 2025. The highest-quality studies included in the review found no evidence supporting a causal relationship between vaccines and autism spectrum disorder. "Accurate information is essential, but information alone does not always change a decision. When people decide whether to get vaccinated or vaccinate their children, they are also influenced by how much they trust the source, the experiences of people close to them, family and community norms, fear, and the messages they repeatedly encounter on social media. That is why responding to a myth requires more than presenting facts. We also need to listen to the concerns behind it and respond without judgement," explains Cristina Stratulat, Social and Behaviour Change Officer at UNICEF Moldova. UNICEF/2026/Moldova HPV vaccines have been used for more than a decade "The vaccine is too new and hasn't been properly tested." This is another myth circulating among young people and creating uncertainty. In fact, HPV vaccines have been used worldwide for more than a decade, with continuous safety monitoring and hundreds of millions of doses administered. The link between HPV and cervical cancer became clear in the 1980s, when research by German virologist Harald zur Hausen led to the identification of HPV types 16 and 18 in cancerous tissue. This discovery, for which he received the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 2008, fundamentally transformed our understanding of cervical cancer and paved the way for the development of preventive vaccines. UNICEF/2026/Moldova How does the HPV vaccine actually work? "The HPV vaccine does not contain a live virus. Instead, it contains virus-like particles without viral genetic material, which means they cannot cause infection. Their purpose is to train the immune system to recognise certain types of HPV and develop protection against them before the body comes into contact with the virus," explains Angela Capcelea, Health Specialist at UNICEF Moldova. UNICEF/2026/Moldova More about the history of HPV, prevention and the role of vaccination can also be explored in a documentary produced by UNICEF and the Ministry of Health of the Republic of Moldova, in partnership with the National Agency for Public Health and the World Health Organization in Moldova, with financial support from the Government of France. The documentary is part of the National Social and Behaviour Change Plan for Immunization 2027 and explains, in accessible language, how our understanding of HPV has evolved and how prevention can help protect people's health. Why HPV vaccination is recommended before exposure to the virus Another belief Ludmila has encountered in her community is that vaccination is "too early" for children or adolescents. "Some people also believe that the vaccine is not safe for children. In fact, vaccination is recommended at a young age, before potential exposure to the virus, precisely because it provides the most effective protection," she says. And Ludmila is right. The vaccine does not change sexual behaviour. It provides medical protection, just like other vaccines. The reason HPV vaccination is recommended at a young age is prevention: the vaccine is most effective when administered before exposure to the virus. This is not an assumption about when an adolescent might become sexually active, but rather a way to establish protection well in advance. UNICEF/2026/Moldova HPV vaccines have been used worldwide for nearly two decades. By early 2025, more than 500 million doses had been distributed globally, and safety studies involving millions of people had identified no new safety concerns. In the Republic of Moldova, HPV vaccination was introduced into the National Immunization Schedule in 2017, initially for girls. Since 2021, it has also been available to boys. In 2025, the vaccination schedule was simplified, and access was expanded to include women up to the age of 26. Despite these developments, vaccination coverage remains low. According to the latest figures reported by the Ministry of Health, just over 46 per cent of girls aged 10–14 have been vaccinated against HPV, compared with approximately 4 per cent of boys. Increasing vaccination coverage, alongside screening and timely treatment, is essential to achieving the goal of eliminating cervical cancer as a public health problem. How is vaccine safety maintained? Vaccine safety is ensured throughout the entire process, from procurement to administration. Vaccines are transported and stored under controlled temperatures, between +2°C and +8°C, while monitoring systems continuously verify that the cold chain is maintained. What can we learn from countries with long-standing HPV vaccination programmes? For Roman, from Căușeni, one of the most effective ways to address myths is to show what has happened in countries where HPV vaccination has been used for many years. "Myths about the HPV vaccine can be challenged with evidence and concrete examples. The vaccine is not new. It has been used for more than a decade and has been administered to a very large number of people," says Roman. The experience of countries with long-established vaccination programmes already demonstrates significant results. In the United Kingdom, the HPV vaccination programme was introduced in 2008. Subsequent studies have shown substantial reductions in precancerous lesions and cervical cancer among generations vaccinated at a young age. Australia introduced HPV vaccination nationwide in 2007 and later expanded the programme to include boys. The country has recorded major reductions in infections caused by vaccine-targeted HPV types and in precancerous lesions. It is among the countries making the greatest progress towards eliminating cervical cancer as a public health problem. These results demonstrate the impact vaccination can have when supported by high coverage, regular screening and access to treatment. Prevention, however, does not end with vaccination. Cervical screening remains essential for detecting and treating precancerous lesions before they develop into cancer. UNICEF/2022/Moldova/VladimirDogoter Vaccination coverage remains uneven Despite progress, substantial disparities remain between countries. Globally, approximately 33 per cent of girls had received at least one dose of the HPV vaccine in 2025. While this represents an increase compared with previous years, coverage remains well below the target set for 2030. The World Health Organization's strategy to eliminate cervical cancer as a public health problem sets three targets to be achieved by 2030: 90 per cent of girls fully vaccinated against HPV by the age of 15; 70 per cent of women screened using a high-performance test; and 90 per cent of women diagnosed with precancerous lesions or cancer receiving the necessary treatment. In the Republic of Moldova, modelling conducted before the HPV vaccine was introduced also highlighted the potential impact of high vaccination coverage. A cost-effectiveness study carried out in 2016 using WHO methodology estimated that vaccinating 80 per cent of girls aged 10–12 could prevent 127 cases of cervical cancer and 98 deaths associated with the disease. Accurate information matters. But so does who delivers it. At Summer School, the young participants were not trained to become "mini-doctors". Their role is different: to start conversations, recognise myths, share evidence-based information responsibly and guide their peers towards trustworthy sources and health services. This was one of the key objectives of the HPV component of the Summer School. "Peer education does not mean that young people need to become health experts or make decisions on behalf of their peers. Their role is to create a space where other adolescents feel comfortable asking questions, identifying and correcting misinformation using reliable sources and, when necessary, seeking support from a health professional or health service. Being close in age and speaking the same language can sometimes make that first conversation easier," adds Cristina Stratulat, Social and Behaviour Change Officer at UNICEF Moldova. UNICEF/2026/Moldova/DanSaulea Victoria believes that hearing information from someone of a similar age can make a difference in how it is received. "It's different when information comes from a teacher compared with when it comes from a friend your own age. I think I would use real-life examples because they help us better understand the consequences the virus can have and the fact that it can affect anyone." Dumitrița sees similar potential in the online space. "Even a message that seems small can make a difference. If it comes from someone well-known or influential, it can reach a much wider audience. We live in a digital age, and young people spend a lot of time on their phones watching reels. That's why social media posts and people they trust can help bring a topic to more people's attention and get conversations started." Taking the conversation further – into schools, families and communities The Summer School may have ended, but for the volunteers, the work of sharing what they have learned is only beginning. Roman hopes to organise activities with students and talk to them about HPV. Vlad plans to use both the information and the interactive methods he learned in Holercani with his classmates and throughout his school. Victoria wants to raise the topic at school and during activities for young people in her community. Dumitrița is also considering social media campaigns. "I would like to organise information sessions together with other young people. Since I'm very active on social media, I'd also love to run online campaigns to raise awareness and help others learn more about these topics," she says. Questions about HPV may begin with something heard from a friend or parent, or seen in an online video. Sometimes, the absence of questions comes from the belief that "it couldn't happen to me". As the volunteers discovered in Holercani, challenging a myth can begin with a conversation. And a conversation grounded in trust and evidence can lead to a more informed decision. Have questions about HPV or vaccination? Talk to your family doctor or the specialists at your nearest Youth Klinic centre, and always check information against reliable medical sources. The 11th edition of the Youth Klinic Moldova Summer School for Volunteers and Volunteer Coordinators was organised by UNICEF and the NGO Health for Youth, with financial support from the Government of Germany through the KfW Development Bank, and support from the Government of the United Kingdom, within the framework of the National Sexual and Reproductive Health and Rights Programme 2023–2027. The Summer School also received support from ERIKS Development Partner and the World Health Organization and was held under the auspices of the Ministry of Health. content_title: HPV vaccines protect against cancer. Could they benefit pregnancy?
content: A nationwide study of more than 624,000 births suggests HPV vaccination may offer benefits beyond cancer prevention, with women vaccinated before age 17 showing 10% lower odds of preterm birth and 11% lower odds of spontaneous preterm birth. Study: Quadrivalent human papillomavirus vaccination before pregnancy and pregnancy outcomes: nationwide, population based case-control study. Image credit: Prostock-studio/Shutterstock.com Preterm birth is a major contributor to neonatal mortality and later health sequelae in adulthood. A recent nationwide Swedish study in the journal BMJ found that the quadrivalent human papillomavirus ( HPV ) vaccine was associated with modestly lower odds of several adverse pregnancy outcomes, especially when given earlier in life. Could HPV vaccination help reduce adverse pregnancy outcomes? Despite its substantial medical and social burden, preterm birth remains difficult to prevent, with limited effective interventions available. Emerging evidence suggests that human papillomavirus (HPV) infection may contribute to preterm birth and other adverse pregnancy outcomes, raising the possibility of a preventable risk factor. In addition to the potential effects of infection itself, surgical excision of HPV-related precancerous and early cancerous cervical lesions has been associated with an increased risk of adverse pregnancy outcomes. These procedures are particularly relevant because cervical lesions and their treatment often occur during the reproductive years. HPV vaccination could therefore offer reproductive health benefits beyond its established role in preventing cervical precancer and cancer. In Sweden, HPV vaccination was introduced in 2006, followed by subsidized vaccination for adolescent girls and, subsequently, a school-based program. Vaccination at younger ages provides particularly strong protection against HPV infection and its associated complications. Early studies have suggested that HPV vaccination before pregnancy may also reduce the risk of adverse pregnancy outcomes; however, evidence remains limited. Even modest reductions in pregnancy complications could translate into meaningful public health benefits given the widespread uptake of HPV vaccination. Against this background, the current study examined the association between quadrivalent HPV vaccination before pregnancy and adverse pregnancy outcomes using nationwide Swedish registry data. By linking individual vaccination records with pregnancy outcomes and other maternal characteristics, the researchers sought to provide more robust evidence on these associations, including whether they differed according to age at vaccination. Swedish study examines HPV vaccination and pregnancy outcomes The study population included 624,713 nulliparous women aged 16-35 years who gave birth to singleton infants at 22 or more completed weeks of gestation in Sweden between 2006 and 2023. Of these, almost 15% had received the quadrivalent HPV vaccine before pregnancy. Women who immigrated to Sweden after age nine were excluded, as were those whose first recorded HPV vaccination before childbirth involved the bivalent or nonavalent vaccine, those vaccinated after conception, and those with missing gestational age information. The primary outcomes assessed included preterm birth and spontaneous preterm birth ( sPTB ). Other secondary outcomes were noted, including preterm prelabor rupture of membranes ( pPROM ), prelabor rupture of membranes ( PROM ) at term, small for gestational age ( SGA ) and severe SGA infant (birth weight below the 10th and 3rd percentiles, respectively, for gestational age and sex), stillbirth, and neonatal mortality. Preterm birth was stratified by gestational age at birth, as extremely preterm (22-<28 weeks), very preterm (28-<32 weeks), and moderate-to-late preterm (32-<37 weeks). Cases were matched to up to ten controls by maternal age at childbirth and calendar year of conception, as these factors affected vaccination rates. The researchers compared women who had received at least one dose of quadrivalent HPV vaccination before conception with those who had not. Confounding factors were adjusted for, including smoking, age at childbirth, body mass index, and assisted reproduction. Details of cervical cancer or precancerous lesions were retrieved from the national registry. HPV vaccination linked to lower odds of preterm birth Vaccinated women were more likely to give birth in the most recent years, were younger at the time of childbirth, and were more likely to have Swedish-born mothers. Among the unvaccinated, 3.7% of mothers had a high-grade cervical lesion diagnosed before childbirth, compared to 0.6% of the vaccinated population. In the adjusted analyses, vaccination was associated with lower odds of all adverse pregnancy outcomes. However, these associations were statistically significant for only some outcomes. The odds were 5% lower each for preterm birth and sPTB, and 15% lower for very preterm birth. The odds of secondary outcomes such as pPROM were 7% lower, and the odds of severe SGA were 8% lower. These associations were also statistically significant, although the confidence interval for pPROM reached 1.00 after rounding. The adjusted associations for extremely preterm birth, moderate-to-late preterm birth, PROM at term, SGA, stillbirth, and neonatal mortality did not reach statistical significance. However, the associations for preterm birth, sPTB, and pPROM were attenuated towards the null when adjusted for history of a high-grade cervical lesion. At the same time, estimates for other outcomes changed minimally. The authors note this is an exploratory analysis, as diagnosis does not imply treatment occurred or define the type and timing of treatment. Vaccination before age 17 shows stronger protective associations Women vaccinated before age 17 had lower odds of the primary outcomes, with 10% and 11% lower odds of preterm birth and sPTB, respectively. Among secondary outcomes, statistically significant associations were observed for pPROM and severe SGA, with odds reduced by 14% and 9%, respectively. For women vaccinated at later ages, statistically significant associations were observed only for severe SGA, by 7%, and stillbirth, by 21%. Moreover, when earlier versus later vaccination were compared for odds of adverse outcomes, all adjusted odds ratio estimates were lower for the group vaccinated earlier except for SGA and stillbirth, and significantly lower for preterm birth, sPTB, and pPROM. Swedish findings reinforce earlier evidence on pregnancy outcomes Sensitivity analyses produced results largely consistent with the main findings. The researchers also estimated the number needed to treat ( NNT ) using model-based absolute risks from a population-based cohort analysis. The lowest estimates, ranging from 451 to 573, were observed for severe SGA, preterm birth, PROM, sPTB, and SGA, while the highest was 24,116 for neonatal mortality. However, because these estimates were derived from observational data, they do not establish how many women would need to be vaccinated to prevent one adverse outcome. The findings are consistent with two earlier Finnish studies based on a community-randomized HPV vaccination trial, which reported lower rates of preterm birth among vaccinated women. However, both studies were limited by small numbers of pregnancies and follow-up restricted to early reproductive age. Evidence from other countries has been mixed. A Danish study found a lower risk of sPTB among women vaccinated before age 17, but not among those vaccinated later. Meanwhile, a Scottish study found no association between HPV vaccination and preterm birth. However, vaccination was linked to lower risks of pPROM, PROM, antepartum hemorrhage, and pre-eclampsia, with considerable variation in effect sizes. An Australian population-level study also reported 3.2% lower rates of preterm birth and 9.8% lower rates of SGA births among maternal cohorts with HPV vaccination coverage of 60%-80%. However, these findings could not establish a protective effect at the individual level, and residual confounding, particularly from smoking, could not be ruled out. The current study builds on this evidence by matching women according to maternal age and calendar year of conception. This approach helped account for changes over time in HPV vaccine availability and uptake, cervical screening practices, obstetric care, and the recording of pregnancy outcomes. HPV prevention may reduce pregnancy complications through two pathways The proposed mechanisms for the observed protective associations include prevention of HPV infection of the cervix and reduced excisional procedures on the cervix for HPV-related lesions. Regarding the first, some studies suggest embryonic development is affected by HPV exposure, perhaps contributing to preterm birth risk via poor placental development. Moreover, the risk of sPTB is approximately twice as high among women who had excisional treatment for high-grade cervical lesions. Meta-analysis findings show increased risks of low birth weight, preterm birth, and PROM after cervical conization is performed. Together, these epidemiological, clinical, and experimental findings provide biologically plausible explanations for the observed associations. However, the present study could not directly establish whether prevention of HPV infection or reduced cervical procedures accounted for the lower odds of adverse pregnancy outcomes. Limitations The study's strengths included its large size and high-quality nationwide registry data, long follow-up periods, careful matching by calendar year and maternal age, and adjustment for multiple confounders. Despite this, the study had several limitations. Residual confounding may have persisted despite extensive adjustments, mainly because the study was observational. Opportunistic or catch-up HPV vaccination may have occurred after HPV infection, potentially weakening the observed associations and contributing to residual confounding. Other possible issues include the inability to identify differences in health-seeking behavior and reproductive or sexual behavior, as well as differences in the use of cerclage and other interventions to prevent preterm birth. Spontaneous abortions before 22 weeks were not captured, though they represent competing events for preterm birth and related outcomes, potentially influencing the observed associations. Overlap between intrapartum stillbirth and sPTB remained unresolved. Finally, post-vaccination HPV infection and cervical treatment were not captured, preventing direct investigation of the proposed biological and clinical mechanisms. Statistical power was also limited for certain rare outcomes, particularly stillbirth and neonatal mortality. Contextual differences in HPV prevalence, infection rates, and high-grade cervical lesions, as well as vaccination programs and obstetric care, may affect the generalizability of the findings. Early HPV vaccination may offer additional reproductive benefits The study suggests a modest reduction in the adjusted odds of several adverse pregnancy outcomes after quadrivalent HPV vaccination before pregnancy. The most marked decrease in odds occurred among women vaccinated at earlier ages. “Together with previous research showing the safety of human papillomavirus vaccination during pregnancy, our results suggest that human papillomavirus vaccination is not only safe with respect to pregnancy outcomes but may also confer additional benefits by reducing the risk of adverse events.” The authors cite this as evidence supporting continued routine HPV vaccination. Future studies should involve long-term follow-up of vaccinated groups, monitoring pregnancy and birth outcomes, to better assess the actual breadth and magnitude of the impact of these changes and clarify the mechanisms that might explain the observed associations. Journal reference: Zhang, Z., Ploner, A., Sengpiel, V., et al. (2026). Quadrivalent human papillomavirus vaccination before pregnancy and pregnancy outcomes: nationwide, population based case-control study. BMJ . Experts at Rutgers New Jersey Medical School and University Hospital note the estimate underscores the importance of awareness, prevention and early detection, which can play a critical role in improving health outcomes. This team of gynecologic specialists – Ana Tergas, Lisa Gabor, Nancy Zhou and Udele Tagoe – brings together clinical expertise, research and commitment to patient-centered care, working collaboratively to address the needs of women throughout diagnosis and treatment in the greater Newark area. Together, in collaboration with Rutgers Cancer Institute, the state’s only National Cancer Institute–designated Comprehensive Cancer Center, they offer a team-based approach that connects specialized knowledge and individualized care. Members of the team discuss gynecologic cancers, symptoms women may overlook and the importance of early detection. How do the five main gynecologic cancers – uterine, cervical, ovarian, vaginal and vulvar – differ in terms of symptoms, risk factors and treatment? Gabor: Gynecologic cancers have overlapping symptoms and risk factors. Increasing age is a risk factor across the board, while smoking is particularly associated with cervical and vulvar cancers. Uterine and ovarian cancers can be linked to hereditary cancer syndromes, such as hereditary breast and ovarian cancer and Lynch syndrome, so personal and family histories of cancer may increase risk. Human papillomavirus infection is particularly important in the development of cervical, vulvar and vaginal cancers. These cancers can all present with abnormal vaginal or postmenopausal bleeding. Ovarian cancer has notoriously vague symptoms, including abdominal distention or bloating, changes in weight or appetite and abdominal or pelvic pain. Treatment may involve surgery, chemotherapy and radiation with the goal of maximizing success while minimizing side effects. What are some gynecologic cancer symptoms that women might overlook? Tergas: Since many symptoms of gynecologic cancers overlap with benign conditions, they may be overlooked. Any bleeding after menopause warrants prompt investigation. Changes in menstrual patterns, especially heavy or uncontrolled bleeding, should also be evaluated. Persistent irritation, nonhealing wounds or ulcers of the vagina or vulva – especially when symptoms do not improve with treatment – require a thorough exam and possible biopsy. Ovarian cancer symptoms may include bloating, decreased appetite, fatigue and weight loss, especially with a family history of cancer. Cervical cancer is the only gynecologic cancer with a routine screening test. What can women do to remain proactive about their health? Tagoe: High-risk human papillomavirus infection causes more than 90% of cervical cancers. While most young, healthy individuals clear the virus spontaneously, persistent infection can cause precancerous changes that may progress into cervical cancer. Since HPV usually causes no symptoms, screening is an important tool in prevention. The Pap and high-risk human papillomavirus tests identify precancerous changes of the cervix. Women should discuss the appropriate screening strategy with their health care provider. The HPV vaccine protects against types responsible for most cervical cancers. Most importantly, stay up to date with screening and follow up on abnormal results. Cervical cancer is highly preventable when HPV vaccination, screening and timely treatment of precancerous changes are combined. How can early detection make a significant difference in treatment options? Zhou: Routine cervical cancer screening can detect precancerous changes, which can often be monitored or treated before they develop into cancer. Early detection expands treatment options. Treating precancerous changes is important for prevention and preserving fertility. Treatment can often be limited to removing the abnormal area while preserving the uterus and fertility. Women should not wait for symptoms to seek screening, because precancer and early cervical cancer may not cause symptoms. Staying up to date with screening and promptly following up on abnormal results can make a meaningful difference in prevention and treatment. How are Rutgers Cancer Institute and University Hospital advancing research, treatment and patient care in gynecologic oncology? Tergas: At Rutgers and University Hospital, women facing gynecologic cancers have access to an academic medical center with experienced specialists that work collaboratively with the state’s only National Cancer Institute-designated Comprehensive Cancer Center – Rutgers Cancer Institute. right in their community. Our gynecologic oncologists provide full-spectrum care, including robotic and minimally invasive surgery, radical debulking surgery, chemotherapy and the latest targeted therapies. We work within a multidisciplinary team to develop a coordinated plan tailored to each patient, who may also access clinical trials of promising new therapies. Our goal is to care for the whole person by pairing expert medical treatment with supportive services such as nutrition and rehabilitation, fertility preservation counseling, palliative care and emotional and social support. What is one message you would like women to take away about gynecologic cancer? Zhou: Do not wait. Pay close attention to your body and act on what it tells you. Many gynecologic cancers can be prevented or caught early, when they are most treatable, but only if women stay up to date on preventive care and seek care for symptoms that are new, persistent or unusual. Early action can save lives. More CLINICAL QUESTION In human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccine–naive patients undergoing cervical conization (cone biopsy) for cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN), does HPV vaccination administered shortly before or after the procedure reduce recurrent high-grade cervical dysplasia compared with no HPV vaccination? EVIDENCE-BASED ANSWER HPV vaccination administered to HPV vaccine–naive patients around the time of conization may reduce recurrent CIN grade 2 or higher (CIN 2+) at 24 to 36 months compared with no vaccination.1 It is unclear whether HPV vaccination at the time of conization prevents CIN 3+ or whether invasive cervical cancer is reduced. Vaccine-related harms were incompletely reported, but those harms reported appeared to be mostly mild. (Strength of Recommendation: B, inconsistent or limited-quality patient-oriented evidence.) PRACTICE POINTERS Cervical cancer remains a major global health concern and is the fifth most commonly diagnosed cancer in women globally.2 The American Cancer Society estimated there would be approximately 13,490 new cases of invasive cervical cancer and approximately 4,200 deaths from cervical cancer in 2026 in the United States.3 CIN, a precancerous condition typically caused by persistent infection with oncogenic HPV types, is treated to prevent progression to invasive cervical cancer, most often with excisional biopsy (eg, conization). After excisional treatment, patients remain at risk of recurrent CIN or invasive cervical cancer and require ongoing surveillance. Primary prevention of cervical cancer is most commonly achieved via HPV vaccination before HPV exposure. Population-level evidence shows that HPV vaccination reduces cervical cancer incidence by approximately 80% when given at or before age 16 years, while also reducing high-grade cervical precancerous lesions (eg, CIN 2 or 3).4 Although prophylactic vaccination is highly effective for primary prevention, its role as an adjuvant strategy in HPV vaccine–naive patients around the time of conization for CIN 2 or 3 is uncertain. This Cochrane review included 13 studies (two randomized controlled trials and 11 nonrandomized studies) including 21,453 HPV vaccine–naive patients undergoing conization for CIN.1 Studies were conducted in Europe (10 studies), China, South Korea, and Iran; none were conducted in the United States.1 HPV vaccines included bivalent, quadrivalent, and nonavalent formulations; comparator groups received no HPV vaccination.1 Follow-up was up to 36 months in randomized trials and beyond 60 months in some nonrandomized studies. Follow-up settings (ie, primary care or specialty clinics) were not consistently reported. Across the two randomized controlled trials (n = 420 participants), recurrent CIN 2+ at 24 to 36 months occurred in 233 per 1,000 patients who did not receive HPV vaccination and 93 per 1,000 patients who did receive vaccination (relative risk =0.40; low-certainty evidence; absolute risk reduction = 140 per 1,000 [14%]; number needed to treat = 8).1 Evidence from nonrandomized studies showed a similar direction of effect, and the review notes that direction of effect for CIN 2+ was generally consistent despite heterogeneity in effect size. However, evidence for CIN 3+ recurrence, persistent HPV infection, and invasive cervical cancer remains very uncertain, with inconsistent findings across nonrandomized studies. Subgroup analyses identified no differences among vaccine types. Vaccine timing and dosing varied across studies (six studies reported that at least 68% of vaccinated participants received three doses, and several studies did not report on dosing completion). Optimal timing remains uncertain. The review authors could not conduct timing-based subgroup analyses, but one large nonrandomized study (n = 17,128) showed a lower recurrence risk among patients vaccinated before conization (within 3 months), whereas patients vaccinated after conization (up to 12 months) had a similar risk to unvaccinated patients. content: Press play to listen to this content Plays:-Audio plays count 1x Playback Speed - 0.5 - 0.6 - 0.7 - 0.8 - 0.9 - 1 - 1.1 - 1.2 - 1.3 - 1.5 - 2 Open text INFECTION-ATTRIBUTABLE cancer caused 2.3 million cases globally in 2024, representing twelve percent of all diagnosed malignancies. A comprehensive worldwide analysis evaluating twelve oncogenic pathogens established that infectious agents remain a major preventable cause of cancer morbidity. While overall global age-standardized incidence reached 22.7 cases per 100,000 person-years, low-income and middle-income regions bore more than three-quarters of the entire disease burden. Eastern Asia recorded the largest absolute caseload with 990,000 cases, while sub-Saharan Africa demonstrated the highest proportional impact, where pathogens drove a quarter of all diagnosed malignancies. Pathogen Distribution in Infection-Attributable Cancer. Two primary pathogens drove nearly two-thirds of the total infectious oncologic burden. Helicobacter pylori accounted for 760,000 cases, primarily causing non-cardia gastric adenocarcinoma and related gastrointestinal cancer sequelae. Human papillomavirus followed closely with 750,000 cases, responsible for all 600,000 cases of cervical cancer alongside substantial fractions of anal, penile, vulvar, vaginal, and oropharyngeal malignancies. Hepatitis B virus contributed 360,000 cases, predominantly hepatocellular carcinoma and intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma. Epstein-Barr virus generated 260,000 cases, emerging as the fourth leading pathogen due to established links with nasopharyngeal carcinoma, gastric adenocarcinoma, and diverse lymphoma subtypes. Hepatitis C virus generated 160,000 malignancies. Additional oncogenic agents included Kaposi sarcoma-associated herpesvirus, human T-cell lymphotropic virus type 1, Merkel cell polyomavirus, Schistosoma haematobium, liver flukes, and HIV. Clinical Priorities and Infection Control. Managing infection-attributable cancer requires aggressive primary prevention alongside expanded diagnostic screening across primary care systems. Proven tools such as routine immunization against human papillomavirus and hepatitis B yield substantial risk reductions when widely implemented. Early detection of gastric precursors through screen-and-treat protocols for bacterial infection offers measurable clinical efficacy, mirroring successful endoscopic protocols in East Asia. Expanding access to direct-acting antivirals for viral hepatitis, promoting barrier protection, and providing long-acting pre-exposure prophylaxis for populations vulnerable to retroviral transmission further curb oncogenic progression. Clinicians must maintain heightened vigilance regarding oncogenic infectious etiologies, integrating vaccination status reviews and targeted pathogen screening into standard preventive adult care. Register FirstWord HEALTHTECH FirstWord REPORTS FirstWord AI FirstWord Pharma Register Sign In Pharma+ News Insight, Analysis & Views StoryWatch Events Resources More FW FirstWord AINEW Top Story Save BioNTech's HPV-targeted cancer vaccine misses PFS goal Anna Bratulic Published : October 13, 2026 Ref: GlobeNewswire, Reuters BioNTech's experimental mRNA cancer immunotherapy BNT113 (tenumomeran/raplemomeran) failed to significantly improve progression-free survival (PFS) when combined with Merck & Co.'s Keytruda (pembrolizumab) in patients with advanced head and neck cancer. Investors reacted by sending the German biotech's US-listed shares down more than 5% on Tuesday, marking a setback for its mRNA cancer vaccine ambitions. The Phase II/III AHEAD-MERIT trial is evaluating the combo as a first-line treatment for patients with unresectable recurrent or metastatic HPV16-positive head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC) whose tumours express PD-L1. The investigational immunotherapy encodes the HPV16-derived E6 and E7 proteins, which are frequently expressed by HPV16-positive solid tumours. OS still in play The study compared BNT113 plus Keytruda with Keytruda alone and has dual primary endpoints of PFS and overall survival (OS). Although the combination missed the PFS endpoint, an independent data monitoring committee recommended continuing the study to assess OS. BioNTech noted that under the prespecified statistical design, a significant improvement in OS could establish a positive trial outcome despite the PFS miss. The company didn't disclose numerical PFS data in Tuesday's announcement. "While the PFS result was not statistically significant at this first analysis, the data support continued evaluation of BNT113 plus pembrolizumab in this trial and show that it is engaging its intended therapeutic mechanism," said Chief Medical Officer Özlem Türeci. "As immune-mediated antitumour effects build and deepen over time, the analysis of the second dual primary endpoint, overall survival, will be critical to fully assess the potential of this approach." How is Big Pharma adapting to China’s rise and the looming patent cliff? Join FirstWord Pharma’s editorial team to examine how industry leaders are responding to two major forces reshaping the competitive landscape. Limits to added benefit? However, Citi analyst Geoffrey Meacham suggested that the cancer's biology could make it difficult for BNT113 to improve on Keytruda's efficacy. "While disappointing, ​HNSCC is heterogeneous and heavily immunosuppressed, making ​incremental efficacy over pembrolizumab challenging despite the HPV16 target," he said. BioNTech's mRNA oncology efforts have yielded mixed results. In late August, the company and Roche's Genentech unit decided to terminate a Phase II trial of the individualised cancer immunotherapy autogene cevumeran (BNT122) in patients with resected colorectal cancer and detectable circulating tumour DNA after an independent monitoring board had flagged a "numerical imbalance" in OS between patient groups in the study. However, there was better news last month when BioNTech and partner OncoC4 reported median OS of 18.5 months with the investigational immunotherapy gotistobart (BNT316/ONC-392) versus 10 months with chemotherapy in previously treated squamous non–small-cell lung cancer, based on the non-pivotal first stage of the Phase III PRESERVE-003 trial. content: Skip to content North American Community Hub Statistics Home US Population News Blog Demographics Disease Data Hospital Data Birth and Fertility Mortality U.S Maps Cities Population States More About Us Editorial Policy Contact Us Home US Population News Blog Demographics Disease Data Hospital Data Birth and Fertility Mortality U.S Maps Cities Population States More About Us Editorial Policy Contact Us Search Discover more Study Biology Check Symptoms infectious WHO Cancer Study Finds 12% of New Cases Linked to Infections, With Stomach Bacteria Leading the List Carter Anderson Published: October 14, 2026 Updated: October 14, 2026 Blog, Disease Data, Mortality, News Discover more cancers cancer Cancer A common stomach bacterium and a virus that many people encounter during their lives were responsible for an estimated 1.5 million new cancer cases worldwide in 2024, according to new research from the World Health Organization. The study found that infections caused about 2.3 million of the 20 million new cancer cases diagnosed worldwide that year. That means around one in eight cancer cases was linked to a virus, bacterium or parasite. Researchers examined 12 infections known to cause cancer. The biggest surprise was that a bacterium called Helicobacter pylori, or H. pylori, was linked to slightly more cancer cases than HPV, the virus widely associated with cervical cancer. The findings were published on September 28, 2026, in The Lancet Oncology by researchers from the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC), part of the WHO. Many of the infections identified in the study can be prevented or treated. Vaccines already protect against HPV and hepatitis B, and antibiotics can eliminate H. pylori. Doctors also have tests that can find some infections and early signs of cancer before serious illness develops. Discover more Cancers Find Cancer Care infection Table of Contents Toggle Stomach Bacteria and HPV Were Linked to the Most Cancer Cases Hepatitis B and C Were Linked to More Than 500,000 Cancer Cases Epstein-Barr Virus Was Also Linked to 260,000 Cases Eastern Asia Had the Most Cancer Cases Linked to Infections What Can People Do to Lower the Risk? Does the Study Mean 2.3 Million Cancer Cases Could Have Been Prevented? How Researchers Estimated the 2.3 Million Cases Stomach Bacteria and HPV Were Linked to the Most Cancer Cases HPV was the infection that caused most cases of cancer, according to the study. Image credit: pexels.com/Monstera Production H. pylori was linked to an estimated 760,000 new cancer cases worldwide in 2024, mostly stomach cancer. HPV followed closely with 750,000 cases, including about 600,000 cases of cervical cancer. Together, the two infections caused an estimated 1.51 million cases, or about 66% of all cancers linked to infections in the study. Hepatitis B came next with 360,000 cases, followed by Epstein-Barr virus with 260,000 and hepatitis C with 160,000. Infection Estimated Cancer Cases in 2024 Cancers Commonly Linked to It H. pylori 760,000 Stomach cancer Human papillomavirus (HPV) 750,000 Cervical, throat, anal and other cancers Hepatitis B 360,000 Liver cancer Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) 260,000 Certain lymphomas, throat and stomach cancers Hepatitis C 160,000 Liver cancer Kaposi sarcoma-associated herpesvirus 35,000 Kaposi sarcoma and certain other cancers Other infections studied 19,000 Several less common cancers Source: WHO International Agency for Research on Cancer. The estimates are rounded, so their sum will not exactly equal the reported global total. The study does not mean everyone who catches one of these infections will develop cancer. Most infections never lead to the disease. Cancer generally develops only in a small share of infected people, sometimes after many years. The risk depends on the infection, how long it remains in the body and other health factors. What Is H. pylori and How Can It Cause Stomach Cancer? Video: Dr. Shria Kumar of the University of Miami explains how H. pylori raises stomach cancer risk, particularly among Asian, Hispanic, Black, and Native American populations. H. pylori is a bacterium that lives in the stomach. Many infected people never experience symptoms and do not know they have it. In some people, however, the bacterium irritates the stomach lining and causes ongoing inflammation. It can also cause stomach ulcers. Over many years, the damage caused by a persistent infection can increase the risk of stomach cancer. According to the National Cancer Institute, long-term studies have found that eliminating H. pylori with antibiotics reduces the risk of developing stomach cancer. One large study in China found that treatment reduced stomach cancer cases by nearly half over 22 years of follow-up. Doctors can diagnose H. pylori using breath or stool tests. Treatment generally involves a combination of medicines, including antibiotics, and a follow-up test is used to confirm that the infection has cleared. People with persistent stomach pain, recurring ulcers or a family history of stomach cancer can discuss testing with a healthcare professional. Routine testing decisions depend on symptoms, medical history and individual risk. The WHO findings do not suggest that everyone needs immediate H. pylori testing. They show how treating a known cancer-causing infection can reduce future risk. HPV Was Linked to 750,000 Cancer Cases Worldwide Human papillomavirus, commonly called HPV, is another infection that can lead to cancer years after someone becomes infected. Most HPV infections clear without treatment. When certain high-risk types remain in the body, however, they can cause changes in cells that eventually develop into cancer. HPV causes nearly all cervical cancers. It can also cause cancers of the anus, penis, vagina, vulva and the back of the throat. Unlike H. pylori, HPV has an effective vaccine that protects against several of the virus types responsible for cancer. Vaccination works best before exposure to HPV. Screening is still necessary for people who are eligible because the vaccine does not protect against every cancer-causing HPV type and cannot treat an existing infection. HPV Causes an Estimated 39,300 Cancer Cases Each Year in the United States The new WHO study covers the entire world, but separate American statistics show how seriously HPV affects cancer rates in the United States. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention estimates that HPV causes about 39,300 cancers annually in the United States. That estimate comes from cancer cases recorded between 2018 and 2022. The CDC identified an average of 49,908 cancers each year in parts of the body where HPV is known to cause cancer, then estimated how many were actually caused by the virus. U.S. HPV Cancer Statistic Annual Cases Cancers diagnosed in areas commonly affected by HPV 49,908 Estimated cancers caused by HPV 39,300 Cases linked to HPV types targeted by the nine-valent vaccine 36,400 The CDC estimates that around 36,400 of the cancers caused by HPV each year involve virus types covered by the nine-valent HPV vaccine. Those cancers include cases affecting both men and women. In fact, the CDC estimates that HPV causes about 16,000 cancers of the back of the throat each year in the United States. Around 13,600 of those cases occur in men. Cervical cancer remains one of the most widely recognized HPV-related cancers, but the American figures show that the virus is a concern for both sexes. The 39,300 annual cases are based on American data from 2018 through 2022. They should not be added to the new global figures as though both studies measured the same year. Hepatitis B and C Were Linked to More Than 500,000 Cancer Cases Hepatitis B and hepatitis C are viruses that infect the liver. Both can cause long-term liver damage, including scarring known as cirrhosis. People with chronic hepatitis infection face a higher risk of liver cancer, even if they have few noticeable symptoms during the early stages of the disease. The WHO study linked approximately 360,000 cancer cases to hepatitis B and another 160,000 to hepatitis C in 2024. A vaccine is available for hepatitis B, and effective antiviral treatment can help people living with the infection. Hepatitis C has no approved vaccine, but modern antiviral medicines can cure most infections. The hepatitis B fact sheet by WHO estimates that 240 million people worldwide were living with chronic hepatitis B in 2024. Testing is especially relevant because a person can have chronic hepatitis for years without knowing it. Identifying the infection gives doctors an opportunity to treat it and monitor liver health. Epstein-Barr Virus Was Also Linked to 260,000 Cases Epstein-Barr virus, or EBV, is extremely common. It spreads mainly through saliva and is known for causing infectious mononucleosis, sometimes called mono. Many people become infected during childhood or adolescence. After infection, the virus remains in the body, usually without causing further illness. In a small share of people, EBV contributes to certain cancers, including some lymphomas and cancers affecting the area behind the nose. Researchers have also linked the virus to a share of stomach cancer cases. The new study estimates that EBV caused about 260,000 new cancer cases worldwide in 2024. There is currently no licensed vaccine against EBV. The American Cancer Society explains the links between cancer and several viruses, including EBV, HPV and hepatitis viruses. Having had mono or a positive EBV test does not mean a person is likely to develop cancer. The majority of people infected with EBV never develop an EBV-related cancer. Eastern Asia Had the Most Cancer Cases Linked to Infections Infections caused an estimated 990,000 new cancer cases in Eastern Asia during 2024, representing 42% of the worldwide total. That region includes China, Japan, South Korea and several other countries. The number of cases is influenced by the size of the population, so researchers also compared rates after adjusting for age. Eastern Asia recorded 31.9 infection-related cancer cases per 100,000 people after that adjustment, compared with 22.7 worldwide. Region Cases per 100,000 People Eastern Asia 31.9 Sub-Saharan Africa 28.5 Central and Eastern Europe 24.3 Southeastern Asia 23.1 Worldwide 22.7 Source: IARC global cancer study, based on 2024 estimates. The rates are adjusted for age to make comparisons between regions more meaningful. Stomach cancer associated with H. pylori contributes heavily to the burden in Eastern Asia. In other parts of the world, HPV, hepatitis viruses and infections associated with weakened immune systems contribute larger shares. Access to vaccines, medical testing and treatment also varies considerably from country to country. The regional findings are useful for governments deciding where to expand prevention programs. They do not establish that every individual living in a higher-rate region has the same cancer risk. What Can People Do to Lower the Risk? Some of the infections identified in the WHO study already have proven ways to reduce the chance of developing cancer. The appropriate steps depend on the infection and a person’s age, medical history and exposure risks. HPV vaccination. Vaccines protect against several HPV types that cause cervical, throat and other cancers. People should follow current recommendations and discuss eligibility with their healthcare provider. Cervical cancer screening. HPV testing and other recommended screening can identify infections and cell changes before cervical cancer develops. Hepatitis B vaccination. Vaccination protects against an infection that can cause chronic liver disease and liver cancer. Hepatitis C testing and treatment. Testing can identify an infection that has caused no symptoms. Antiviral medicines can cure most cases. H. pylori testing and treatment. Doctors can test for the bacterium and prescribe treatment when indicated, particularly for people with ulcers or other established risk factors. HIV prevention and treatment. Preventing HIV and maintaining effective treatment helps protect the immune system and reduces the risk of several infection-related cancers. The WHO has set a goal of eliminating cervical cancer as a public health problem. Its global cervical cancer initiative calls for 90% of girls to be vaccinated against HPV by age 15, 70% of women to receive recommended screening by key ages, and 90% of women diagnosed with cervical disease to receive appropriate care. Those targets are intended for countries to reach by 2030. They are not a claim that cervical cancer will disappear worldwide by that date. Does the Study Mean 2.3 Million Cancer Cases Could Have Been Prevented? No. The 2.3 million figure estimates how many cancers were caused by infections in 2024. It does not establish that every one of those cases could have been stopped with the medical tools available today. Some infections have vaccines. but many of them still requires more testing and treatment, while no approved vaccine is available for EBV or hepatitis C. People also face unequal access to care. A vaccine or treatment cannot prevent illness in someone who never receives it, and treating an infection does not guarantee that cancer will never develop. Researchers are describing the number of cancers caused by infections, not reporting the results of a prevention program. The new findings also do not establish that infection-related cancer suddenly increased during 2026. The analysis uses 2024 cancer estimates and was published in September 2026. Earlier studies examined infection-related cancers, but the latest research includes additional infections and newly recognized links to certain cancers. Direct comparisons with older totals therefore require caution. How Researchers Estimated the 2.3 Million Cases Researchers used worldwide cancer estimates for 2024 and existing medical evidence about which infections cause particular cancers. For example, scientists already know that high-risk HPV types cause most cervical cancers. Researchers used that established relationship, together with estimates of cancer diagnoses, to calculate the number linked to HPV. They repeated the process for the other infections, using information about cancer types, infection rates and evidence of causation. The result is an estimate of cancer cases caused by infections across the world. It is not a count of individual patients whose tumors were all tested for bacteria or viruses. There is also uncertainty because countries have unequal access to cancer registries and infection testing. Researchers used the available data to produce estimates for countries and regions where direct information was incomplete. The findings were announced by the International Agency for Research on Cancer on September 29, 2026. Our earlier reporting on the leading causes of death in America examines how the burden of major diseases has changed over time. We have also covered U.S. life expectancy and health trends, including the effects of advances in disease prevention and treatment. content_title: HPV vaccines protect against cancer. Could they benefit pregnancy?
content: A nationwide study of more than 624,000 births suggests HPV vaccination may offer benefits beyond cancer prevention, with women vaccinated before age 17 showing 10% lower odds of preterm birth and 11% lower odds of spontaneous preterm birth. Study: Quadrivalent human papillomavirus vaccination before pregnancy and pregnancy outcomes: nationwide, population based case-control study. Image credit: Prostock-studio/Shutterstock.com Preterm birth is a major contributor to neonatal mortality and later health sequelae in adulthood. A recent nationwide Swedish study in the journal BMJ found that the quadrivalent human papillomavirus ( HPV ) vaccine was associated with modestly lower odds of several adverse pregnancy outcomes, especially when given earlier in life. Could HPV vaccination help reduce adverse pregnancy outcomes? Despite its substantial medical and social burden, preterm birth remains difficult to prevent, with limited effective interventions available. Emerging evidence suggests that human papillomavirus (HPV) infection may contribute to preterm birth and other adverse pregnancy outcomes, raising the possibility of a preventable risk factor. In addition to the potential effects of infection itself, surgical excision of HPV-related precancerous and early cancerous cervical lesions has been associated with an increased risk of adverse pregnancy outcomes. These procedures are particularly relevant because cervical lesions and their treatment often occur during the reproductive years. HPV vaccination could therefore offer reproductive health benefits beyond its established role in preventing cervical precancer and cancer. In Sweden, HPV vaccination was introduced in 2006, followed by subsidized vaccination for adolescent girls and, subsequently, a school-based program. Vaccination at younger ages provides particularly strong protection against HPV infection and its associated complications. Early studies have suggested that HPV vaccination before pregnancy may also reduce the risk of adverse pregnancy outcomes; however, evidence remains limited. Even modest reductions in pregnancy complications could translate into meaningful public health benefits given the widespread uptake of HPV vaccination. Against this background, the current study examined the association between quadrivalent HPV vaccination before pregnancy and adverse pregnancy outcomes using nationwide Swedish registry data. By linking individual vaccination records with pregnancy outcomes and other maternal characteristics, the researchers sought to provide more robust evidence on these associations, including whether they differed according to age at vaccination. Swedish study examines HPV vaccination and pregnancy outcomes The study population included 624,713 nulliparous women aged 16-35 years who gave birth to singleton infants at 22 or more completed weeks of gestation in Sweden between 2006 and 2023. Of these, almost 15% had received the quadrivalent HPV vaccine before pregnancy. Women who immigrated to Sweden after age nine were excluded, as were those whose first recorded HPV vaccination before childbirth involved the bivalent or nonavalent vaccine, those vaccinated after conception, and those with missing gestational age information. The primary outcomes assessed included preterm birth and spontaneous preterm birth ( sPTB ). Other secondary outcomes were noted, including preterm prelabor rupture of membranes ( pPROM ), prelabor rupture of membranes ( PROM ) at term, small for gestational age ( SGA ) and severe SGA infant (birth weight below the 10th and 3rd percentiles, respectively, for gestational age and sex), stillbirth, and neonatal mortality. Preterm birth was stratified by gestational age at birth, as extremely preterm (22-<28 weeks), very preterm (28-<32 weeks), and moderate-to-late preterm (32-<37 weeks). Cases were matched to up to ten controls by maternal age at childbirth and calendar year of conception, as these factors affected vaccination rates. The researchers compared women who had received at least one dose of quadrivalent HPV vaccination before conception with those who had not. Confounding factors were adjusted for, including smoking, age at childbirth, body mass index, and assisted reproduction. Details of cervical cancer or precancerous lesions were retrieved from the national registry. HPV vaccination linked to lower odds of preterm birth Vaccinated women were more likely to give birth in the most recent years, were younger at the time of childbirth, and were more likely to have Swedish-born mothers. Among the unvaccinated, 3.7% of mothers had a high-grade cervical lesion diagnosed before childbirth, compared to 0.6% of the vaccinated population. In the adjusted analyses, vaccination was associated with lower odds of all adverse pregnancy outcomes. However, these associations were statistically significant for only some outcomes. The odds were 5% lower each for preterm birth and sPTB, and 15% lower for very preterm birth. The odds of secondary outcomes such as pPROM were 7% lower, and the odds of severe SGA were 8% lower. These associations were also statistically significant, although the confidence interval for pPROM reached 1.00 after rounding. The adjusted associations for extremely preterm birth, moderate-to-late preterm birth, PROM at term, SGA, stillbirth, and neonatal mortality did not reach statistical significance. However, the associations for preterm birth, sPTB, and pPROM were attenuated towards the null when adjusted for history of a high-grade cervical lesion. At the same time, estimates for other outcomes changed minimally. The authors note this is an exploratory analysis, as diagnosis does not imply treatment occurred or define the type and timing of treatment. Vaccination before age 17 shows stronger protective associations Women vaccinated before age 17 had lower odds of the primary outcomes, with 10% and 11% lower odds of preterm birth and sPTB, respectively. Among secondary outcomes, statistically significant associations were observed for pPROM and severe SGA, with odds reduced by 14% and 9%, respectively. For women vaccinated at later ages, statistically significant associations were observed only for severe SGA, by 7%, and stillbirth, by 21%. Moreover, when earlier versus later vaccination were compared for odds of adverse outcomes, all adjusted odds ratio estimates were lower for the group vaccinated earlier except for SGA and stillbirth, and significantly lower for preterm birth, sPTB, and pPROM. Swedish findings reinforce earlier evidence on pregnancy outcomes Sensitivity analyses produced results largely consistent with the main findings. The researchers also estimated the number needed to treat ( NNT ) using model-based absolute risks from a population-based cohort analysis. The lowest estimates, ranging from 451 to 573, were observed for severe SGA, preterm birth, PROM, sPTB, and SGA, while the highest was 24,116 for neonatal mortality. However, because these estimates were derived from observational data, they do not establish how many women would need to be vaccinated to prevent one adverse outcome. The findings are consistent with two earlier Finnish studies based on a community-randomized HPV vaccination trial, which reported lower rates of preterm birth among vaccinated women. However, both studies were limited by small numbers of pregnancies and follow-up restricted to early reproductive age. Evidence from other countries has been mixed. A Danish study found a lower risk of sPTB among women vaccinated before age 17, but not among those vaccinated later. Meanwhile, a Scottish study found no association between HPV vaccination and preterm birth. However, vaccination was linked to lower risks of pPROM, PROM, antepartum hemorrhage, and pre-eclampsia, with considerable variation in effect sizes. An Australian population-level study also reported 3.2% lower rates of preterm birth and 9.8% lower rates of SGA births among maternal cohorts with HPV vaccination coverage of 60%-80%. However, these findings could not establish a protective effect at the individual level, and residual confounding, particularly from smoking, could not be ruled out. The current study builds on this evidence by matching women according to maternal age and calendar year of conception. This approach helped account for changes over time in HPV vaccine availability and uptake, cervical screening practices, obstetric care, and the recording of pregnancy outcomes. HPV prevention may reduce pregnancy complications through two pathways The proposed mechanisms for the observed protective associations include prevention of HPV infection of the cervix and reduced excisional procedures on the cervix for HPV-related lesions. Regarding the first, some studies suggest embryonic development is affected by HPV exposure, perhaps contributing to preterm birth risk via poor placental development. Moreover, the risk of sPTB is approximately twice as high among women who had excisional treatment for high-grade cervical lesions. Meta-analysis findings show increased risks of low birth weight, preterm birth, and PROM after cervical conization is performed. Together, these epidemiological, clinical, and experimental findings provide biologically plausible explanations for the observed associations. However, the present study could not directly establish whether prevention of HPV infection or reduced cervical procedures accounted for the lower odds of adverse pregnancy outcomes. Limitations The study's strengths included its large size and high-quality nationwide registry data, long follow-up periods, careful matching by calendar year and maternal age, and adjustment for multiple confounders. Despite this, the study had several limitations. Residual confounding may have persisted despite extensive adjustments, mainly because the study was observational. Opportunistic or catch-up HPV vaccination may have occurred after HPV infection, potentially weakening the observed associations and contributing to residual confounding. Other possible issues include the inability to identify differences in health-seeking behavior and reproductive or sexual behavior, as well as differences in the use of cerclage and other interventions to prevent preterm birth. Spontaneous abortions before 22 weeks were not captured, though they represent competing events for preterm birth and related outcomes, potentially influencing the observed associations. Overlap between intrapartum stillbirth and sPTB remained unresolved. Finally, post-vaccination HPV infection and cervical treatment were not captured, preventing direct investigation of the proposed biological and clinical mechanisms. Statistical power was also limited for certain rare outcomes, particularly stillbirth and neonatal mortality. Contextual differences in HPV prevalence, infection rates, and high-grade cervical lesions, as well as vaccination programs and obstetric care, may affect the generalizability of the findings. Early HPV vaccination may offer additional reproductive benefits The study suggests a modest reduction in the adjusted odds of several adverse pregnancy outcomes after quadrivalent HPV vaccination before pregnancy. The most marked decrease in odds occurred among women vaccinated at earlier ages. “Together with previous research showing the safety of human papillomavirus vaccination during pregnancy, our results suggest that human papillomavirus vaccination is not only safe with respect to pregnancy outcomes but may also confer additional benefits by reducing the risk of adverse events.” The authors cite this as evidence supporting continued routine HPV vaccination. Future studies should involve long-term follow-up of vaccinated groups, monitoring pregnancy and birth outcomes, to better assess the actual breadth and magnitude of the impact of these changes and clarify the mechanisms that might explain the observed associations. Journal reference: Zhang, Z., Ploner, A., Sengpiel, V., et al. (2026). Quadrivalent human papillomavirus vaccination before pregnancy and pregnancy outcomes: nationwide, population based case-control study. BMJ . DOI : https://doi.org/10.1136/bmj-2026-100739. https://www.bmj.com/content/395/bmj-2026-100739

content: HPV阳性女性炎症与营养指标与宫颈病变组织病理学严重程度的关联研究 《Bratislava Medical Journal》:Inflammatory and Nutritional Indices Associated with Histopathological Severity of Cervical Lesions in HPV-Positive Women 【字体: 大 中 小 】 时间:2026年10月15日 来源:Bratislava Medical Journal 1.4 为了促进科学的传播,生物通采集了这篇文章 订阅BioHot点这里解锁原文链接推送! “畅读会员”点此登录查看原文链接 Research Open access 本研究旨在评估炎症与营养指标——包括HALP(血红蛋白×白蛋白×淋巴细胞/血小板)、中性粒细胞-淋巴细胞比值(NLR)和系统性免疫炎症指数(SII)——与HPV阳性女性宫颈上皮内瘤变(CIN)分级及浸润性疾病的关联。材料与方法:这项回顾性观察性研究纳入了2020年1月至2025年12月期间接受宫颈活检的122例患者。根据最高组织病理学诊断将患者分为CIN1(n=39)、CIN2(n=30)、CIN3(n=35)和鳞状细胞癌(SCC)(n=18)组。炎症指标(HALP、NLR和SII)根据常规血液学和生化参数计算。采用单因素方差分析(ANOVA)及Tukey事后检验进行组织病理学组间比较。采用多项逻辑回归分析确定组织病理学严重程度的独立预测因子。根据HPV致癌风险分组进行了额外分析,包括高危HPV阴性(HR(-))、高危HPV阳性(HR(+))以及高危和超高危HPV阳性(HR+UHR(+))。结果:年龄、NLR、SII和HALP评分在各组织病理学组间存在显著差异,SCC患者表现为年龄更大、NLR和SII更高、HALP评分更低(p<0.001,p=0.008,p=0.02,p=0.04;分别)。血清白蛋白是区分CIN与SCC的最强独立预测因子(p<0.001)。HPV基因型影响炎症谱,HR(+)与较低的HALP和较高的SII值相关(p=0.002和p=0.03)。在多变量分析中,NLR仅在CIN3–SCC比较中保持独立关联,而HALP和SII未达到统计学显著性。结论:血清白蛋白可能作为与宫颈浸润性疾病相关的潜在生物标志物,但其临床相关性需在更大规模的前瞻性队列中加以证实。HALP、NLR和SII等炎症指标似乎可反映疾病严重程度,但其预测性能可能受HPV致癌风险影响。这些发现提示全身性炎症状态与病毒致癌负荷之间存在潜在相互作用,影响宫颈肿瘤的进展。 论文解读 成熟稳定的基因敲除、基因敲入与点突变、过表达与干扰等基因修饰细胞株构建服务,点击获取详细资料 领 取 一、研究背景与目的 宫颈癌是全球女性最常见的恶性肿瘤之一,在低收入和中等收入国家尤为突出。2020年全球新增宫颈癌病例约604127例,相关死亡341831例,年龄标化发病率和死亡率分别为每10万女性年13.3例和7.2例。高危型人乳头瘤病毒(HPV)感染是宫颈癌发生的核心病因,其中HPV16和HPV18是导致癌前病变进展为浸润癌的主要型别。宫颈上皮内瘤变(CIN)是宫颈癌前病变的组织病理学表现,分为CIN1、CIN2和CIN3三级。近年来,系统性炎症和营养状态被视为癌症生物学的重要决定因素,基于外周血常规参数的炎症营养指标,如HALP评分(血红蛋白×白蛋白×淋巴细胞/血小板)、中性粒细胞-淋巴细胞比值(NLR)和系统性免疫炎症指数(SII),已在多种恶性肿瘤中显示出预后价值。然而,这些指标与CIN分级之间关联的研究仍然有限。识别廉价易得的生物标志物,有助于改善HPV阳性女性的临床风险分层和决策过程。该研究旨在评估HALP、NLR和SII与HPV阳性女性宫颈病变组织病理学严重程度的关联,并探索HPV致癌风险分层的影响。 二、研究方法概述 该研究为回顾性观察性研究,在Bal?kesir大学医学院妇产科进行,纳入了2020年1月至2025年12月期间行宫颈活检的122例患者。纳入标准为具有完整临床和实验室数据的宫颈活检病例,排除血液病、慢性肝病、肾病、自身免疫病、妊娠、合并恶性肿瘤、免疫抑制治疗、铁剂替代治疗以及既往治疗过的宫颈癌等可能影响炎症和营养指标的病例。根据最高组织病理学诊断将患者分为CIN1(n=39)、CIN2(n=30)、CIN3(n=35)和鳞状细胞癌(SCC)(n=18)四组。同时根据HPV基因型致癌风险将患者分为高危HPV阴性(HR(-))、高危HPV阳性(HR(+))、高危和超高危HPV阳性(HR+UHR(+))三组,其中UHR指HPV16和HPV18。炎症指标通过常规全血细胞计数和生化参数计算。统计学方法包括单因素方差分析(ANOVA)及Tukey事后检验、Games-Howell事后检验、多项逻辑回归分析、相关性矩阵和方差膨胀因子(VIF)分析。 三、主要研究结果 1. 组织病理学分组间的参数比较 ANOVA分析显示,年龄、血红蛋白、淋巴细胞计数、血清白蛋白、HALP、SII和NLR在各组织病理学组间存在显著差异。SCC组患者年龄最大(53.39±12.79岁),血红蛋白和淋巴细胞计数最低,血清白蛋白水平显著下降(37.53±7.83 g/L),HALP评分最低(3.65±2.66),而SII和NLR显著升高。Tukey事后检验显示,血清白蛋白的组间差异最为显著,SCC组白蛋白水平明显低于CIN1、CIN2和CIN3组(均p<0.001),而CIN各组间无显著差异。 2. 多项逻辑回归分析 以SCC为参考类别的多项逻辑回归分析显示,血清白蛋白是区分CIN1、CIN2、CIN3与SCC的最强独立预测因子(p<0.001)。年龄仅在CIN3–SCC比较中显著(p=0.008),提示高龄与SCC而非CIN3相关。NLR仅在CIN3–SCC比较中达到统计学显著性(p=0.04),而HALP和SII在所有比较中均未显示独立关联。HPV基因型与组织病理学严重度显著相关,HR HPV(-)在CIN2–SCC和CIN3–SCC比较中与SCC强相关。 3. 共线性诊断与年龄加权分析 VIF分析显示所有连续预测因子的VIF值均小于5,不存在严重共线性。尽管SII与NLR强相关(r=0.87),对应VIF值仍低于阈值。年龄加权分析中,中性粒细胞和血小板计数在组间变得显著,但各炎症指标的统计学显著性水平基本不变。 4. HPV风险分组比较 按HPV基因型分组后,血小板计数、HALP和SII在HPV组间存在显著差异。HR HPV(-)组血小板计数显著低于HR(+)和HR+UHR(+)组。HALP评分在HR HPV(-)组最高,在HR(+)和HR+UHR(+)组显著降低(p=0.002)。SII在HR(+)和HR+UHR(+)组显著升高(p=0.01),尤其是HR+UHR(+)组与HR(-)组差异显著(p=0.03)。年龄、血红蛋白、中性粒细胞、淋巴细胞和NLR在HPV组间无显著差异。 四、讨论与结论 研究人员指出,单变量分析中炎症指标随CIN向SCC进展而升高,支持癌前病变向浸润癌的转变,但多变量回归中部分指标失去显著性,提示这些标志物更反映浸润性疾病而非癌前病变内部的进展。血清白蛋白作为一种负性急性期反应蛋白,在炎症时降低,其作为区分CIN与SCC的最强独立因素,与低白蛋白反映慢性炎症、代谢需求增加和营养状态受损密切相关。HPV基因型分层分析表明,病毒致癌风险水平显著影响全身炎症谱:血小板、HALP和SII的差异提示病毒因素在疾病早期调节宿主炎症反应,而当浸润癌发生时,以白蛋白和NLR为代表的宿主炎症及营养状态在决定组织病理学严重度方面可能优先于HPV基因型。研究人员强调,该研究首次将炎症营养指标与HPV致癌风险分层结合,全面评估从CIN1到浸润癌的病变谱系。研究局限性包括回顾性单中心设计、吸烟状态和体重指数等混杂信息缺失、横断面设计无法确立因果关系,以及SCC病例数较少可能影响模型稳定性。 结论部分指出,该研究凸显了系统性炎症、营养状态与HPV致癌风险在宫颈病变进展中的相互作用。血清白蛋白是区分癌前病变与浸润癌的最显著独立标志物。HALP、NLR和SII等炎症指标可反映疾病严重程度,但受白蛋白水平和HPV型别影响。HR HPV与较低的HALP和较高的SII相关,提示病毒因素调节系统性炎症。年龄和NLR在区分CIN3与SCC方面也具有重要意义。这些发现提示血清白蛋白和炎症标志物在风险评估中具有潜在价值,但在推荐任何临床应用之前,仍需前瞻性研究加以验证。
