content_title: These common infections are linked to 12% of new cancer cases, study says
content: These common infections are linked to 12% of new cancer cases, study says Watch: Trial offers metastatic breast cancer treatment Trial offers metastatic breast cancer treatment WBAL US LIVE Current Time 0:00 / Total Duration 2:11 Sorry, this video is not available, please check back later. Advertisement Updated: 11:02 AM PDT Oct 14, 2026 Editorial Standards i Jacqueline Howard, CNN These common infections are linked to 12% of new cancer cases, study says Updated: 11:02 AM PDT Oct 14, 2026 Editorial Standards i Jacqueline Howard, CNN CNN — Millions of new cancer cases around the world may be caused by infections that are either treatable or preventable, suggesting that the cancer could have been avoided altogether. That's according to new research published in the journal The Lancet Oncology , which found that roughly 1 in 8 cancer cases around the world may be linked to infections – many of which can be prevented through vaccines, screening or relatively straightforward treatments. Advertisement Related video above | Trial offers metastatic breast cancer treatment "We can intervene before it gets anywhere near cancer," said Gary Clifford, the study's senior author and an epidemiologist at the International Agency for Research on Cancer. "We just need the politics and the finances and the buy-in from the public and the communication to get the programs implemented. Prevention works," Clifford said. "It's an awareness-raising issue." About 2.3 million new cancer cases were attributable to infections globally in 2024, which is equivalent to 12% of all cancer diagnoses, the new study found. And two infections stood out in particular: Helicobacter pylori, commonly known as H. pylori, which was mostly associated with gastric cancers and human papillomavirus, or HPV, which was predominantly associated with cervical cancer. Together, researchers estimate that these two infections accounted for more than 1.5 million cancer cases in 2024. Other infections contributed substantially as well: Hepatitis B or HBV was linked to an estimated 360,000 cancer cases, which were mostly liver cancers. The Epstein-Barr virus, or EBV, was associated with about 260,000 cancer cases, of which a head and neck cancer starting in the nasopharynx was the main driver. Hepatitis C or HCV was tied to 160,000 cancer cases, mostly liver cancers. "Some infection-related cancers, such as liver and gastric cancer, generally have poor prognosis, meaning that a similar proportion of deaths from these cancers are likely attributable to infection. For other cancers, including cervical cancer and Kaposi sarcoma, infection is necessary for cancer development," Harriet Rumgay, epidemiologist at the International Agency for Research on Cancer and an author of the study, said in an email. "However, highly effective prevention measures already exist for four of the five leading infectious causes of cancer, as well as for HIV," Rumgay said, referring to the human immunodeficiency virus. The four infections include HPV and hepatitis B, for which vaccines are available, as well as H. pylori and hepatitis C, for which testing and treatments are available. Clifford, Rumgay and their colleagues analyzed data from the Global Cancer Observatory's Cancer Today database to estimate the incidence of cancer around the world in 2024. They examined how many of those cancer cases could be attributable to infections and then analyzed each infection-cancer pair in their data set. The new analysis builds on earlier work published in 2018 , but the researchers now have a better understanding of the relationships between certain infections and cancer. The new study incorporated 16 additional infection-cancer pairs compared with the previous 2018 global analysis, including some cancers paired with EBV. "EBV is one of these agents for which we knew it was related to some cancers. In fact, EBV was the first ever cancer-causing agent of infection to be discovered in Burkitt lymphoma," Clifford said. "That was like 60 years ago almost, and that was the first realization that a virus could cause cancer. And since then, we've identified it in other cancers, particularly nasopharyngeal carcinomas," he said. "We were already clear about the link with EBV, even back in that 2018 data. So, it was there, but it wasn't really fully addressed because we didn't understand the full extent of the cancer burden that it was causing." Where the infection-related cancer burden is greatest The new research also reveals that the burden of infection-related cancers isn't evenly distributed around the world. Low-income and middle-income countries accounted for 77% of all infection-attributable cancer cases, reflecting differences in the prevalence of cancer-causing infections as well as access to vaccines, screening, testing and treatment. But if health officials know which infections are contributing to cancer, and where those infections are most common, they can focus resources on the strategies that have the potential to save lives. "Even within the United States, the burden of infection-related cancer is not evenly distributed, and some populations have higher rates of infections such as hepatitis B, hepatitis C, HPV or H. pylori, while others have less access to vaccination, screening or treatment. And these differences can translate into disparities in cancer incidence many years later," said Veronika Fedirko, professor of epidemiology at The University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center in Houston, who was not involved in the new study. "Infection-related cancers are certainly an important issue in the United States," she said, referring to a separate analysis from the American Cancer Society that found in 2019, 3.4% of all cancers among adults 30 and older – which was about 60,310 cases – were attributable to seven infections evaluated: EBV, H. pylori, hepatitis B, hepatitis C, Kaposi sarcoma-associated herpesvirus, HIV and, the largest contributor, HPV. "Having a cancer-causing infection does not mean that a person will develop cancer. These infections increase the risk of certain cancers, but most people who are infected will never develop cancer," Fedirko said. "Cancer usually develops only in a small proportion of people, often when an infection persists for many years and together with other factors such as age, immune function, smoking, genetics or other exposures." How to 'take away' the risk Cancer is an enormously complicated group of diseases with many different causes and risk factors, including genetics, environmental exposures, aging and lifestyle factors. But the new findings show that infections represent an area where prevention can make a meaningful difference. Prevention efforts can include vaccination and, when appropriate, testing for and treating infections that increase cancer risk. For some cancers, screening can also identify precancerous changes so they can be treated before invasive cancer develops. Getting tested and following up with a doctor "almost takes away any cancer risk," Clifford said. Once infections get diagnosed, "we know how to manage them," he said. "The large majority of these infections will not cause cancer. Some of them will, and we're learning more about which ones, but that's a work in progress. The point is: It doesn't mean that you've got a cancer just because you have the infection." For instance, people can be screened for hepatitis C and treated if they are infected, thus helping to prevent cancer from developing down the road. The same is true for H. pylori. The bacterium is relatively common, and many people who carry it may not immediately realize they have an infection. But H. pylori can cause chronic inflammation in the stomach and become a major risk factor for stomach cancer. Treating the infection with antibiotics can reduce that risk, giving doctors another opportunity to intervene before cancer may develop. Additionally, HPV and hepatitis B are examples of how vaccination can help prevent cancer. Hepatitis B infection can damage the liver over time and increase the risk of liver cancer, but there is a vaccine available that can help prevent the viral infection. HPV is a group of more than 200 related viruses , which can spread through sexual contact. In some cases, HPV infection can lead to six types of cancer : cervical, anal, penile, vaginal, vulvar and oropharyngeal (mouth and throat). But the vaccine can protect against those cancers since it works by preventing HPV infection. The new research "teaches us the importance of vaccination and how that can prevent different types of cancer," Dr. Nancy Lee, a radiation oncologist at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center who was not involved in the new study, said in an email. "This is no different than getting your flu shot to prevent the flu. The public needs to be made aware and vaccination should be reinforced," Lee said. "Many different types of cancers are caused by infection and if we prevent the infection, the incidence of cancer should be lower." Other prevention measures that reduce transmission of various cancer-attributable infections include "safe injection practices, condom use, and HIV pre-exposure prophylaxis," Rumgay said. "If implemented widely and equitably, these strategies could prevent hundreds of thousands, if not millions, of future cancer cases worldwide." content_title: The Nurse Nurturing Vaccine Confidence in an Uzbek Mountain Exclave
content: In Shahimardan, nurse Nilyufar Tursunova says patient explanation of immunisation science is all nervous parents really need. by Umida Maniyazova First published October 6, 2026 by Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance Nilyufar Tursunova shows off her clinic’s insulated vaccine refrigerator. Credit: Umida Maniyazova At a glance Nilyufar Tursunova looks after the 896 children of Shahimardan, a mountain exclave of Uzbekistan. Despite the fact that Shahimardan’s unique geography means that a referral to any larger health centre means crossing an international border twice, she says logistics don’t hamper vaccine uptake in the locality – at least not since her clinic received a reliable vaccine fridge back in 2018. Instead, her major challenge is communicating vaccines well in a climate of anxiety. Her approach is simple: trust the facts to do the talking. “When a mother understands what the vaccine protects her child from, she no longer needs to be persuaded. She makes the decision herself.” “Despite the fact that we are located in an exclave, we have never had difficulties with the delivery of vaccines or with vaccinating children,” says nurse Nilyufar Tursunova of Shahimardan with deserved pride. Shahimardan is part of Uzbekistan, but totally surrounded by Kyrgyzstan, which means that even a routine journey to a larger medical centre involves crossing an international border. That used to pose some problems for reliable vaccine supply, she concedes, but since her clinic got its own vaccine refrigerator back in 2018, the 896 children in her care have never needed to go without. When a mother understands what the vaccine protects her child from, she no longer needs to be persuaded. She makes the decision herself. – Nilyufar Tursunova And that’s even though Shahimardan’s diplomatic reality is not its only geographic challenge. The village lies 1550 m above sea level, ringed by peaks of up to 2,800 m. The rivers Oq-Su and Kok-Su rush along steep valleys; houses seem to cling to the slopes. In the past, when getting kids vaccinated meant going door-to-door, that meant health workers like Tursunova either catching a lift with local residents on old “IZH” motorcycles, Soviet-era bikes fitted with sidecars, or walking house to house along mountain paths. Still, today, vaccine logistics in Shahimardan tick over with little stress or variation. There is only one road leading to the clinic in Shahimardan. Credit: Umida Maniyazova Instead, what most requires Tursunova’s vigilance is the challenge of effectively communicating vaccination. “If you properly explain to parents how vital vaccination is for the child’s healthy development, they understand,” she says. She estimates that 80% of parents here make sure their children receive their vaccines on time. That means that there are still some who are unduly anxious. Gently does it One trigger phrase for the vaccine-worried, Tursunova says, is “live vaccine”. Mothers worry that live vaccines – such as the highly effective and extremely safe live-attenuated measles vaccine – are more liable to provoke fevers and other side-effects than inactivated, or ‘killed’ vaccines. It’s untrue, but could still put parents off immunising their children. That would be dangerous. In 2025, the European Regional Verification Commission concluded that measles transmission had been re-established in Uzbekistan, making continued large-scale vaccination and surveillance all the more important. Still, Tursunova doesn’t respond with pressure. She speaks in a quiet, even voice, soft and unhurried. Eight years of working with children seem to have scrubbed all the sharpness and hurry from her delivery. If it calms down her paediatric patients, it also seems to reach their parents. Once they know what to expect, their concerns usually ease, she says. Tursunova explains what “live-attenuated” really means: that the vaccine uses a weakened, safe form of the virus to stimulate a healthy immune response. But the technical explanation is only part of the task. The way it is communicated matters just as much, she insists. Her faith in kind, respectful conversation has also shaped how Shahimardan has responded to the arrival of unfamiliar vaccines. Shock of the new New vaccines can raise parents’ internal alarm systems. “When we first received the HPV vaccine and started vaccinating girls, there were, of course, some difficulties,” she says. “Not all parents understood what kind of vaccine it was.” In 2019 the human papillomavirus, or HPV, vaccine made its first entrance to Uzbekistan’s vaccine portfolio. The fact that the vaccine, which protects adolescent girls against developing cervical cancer in the future, was being recommended for a different target group than most of the vaccines parents were used to opened the door to anxieties. But over the years, Tursunova says attitudes and knowledge levels have shifted. “Now mothers come themselves and ask: isn’t it time for my daughter to get the vaccine?” At least some of that change appears to be down to Tursunova. For Sayora, the mother of ten-year-old Gulbahor and three younger children, moving to Shahimardan dissolved her resistance to HPV vaccination. When the family lived in Margilan city, about 55 km from Shahimardan, Sayora said neighbours and acquaintances had warned her off having her daughter vaccinated. “People around us used to say that the HPV vaccine could cause infertility and other problems. Many neighbours and acquaintances tried to convince me not to give it to my daughter. I listened to them because I didn’t know enough about the vaccine myself.” The clinic is located on a slope, which helps to protect the critical health infrastructure from mudflows and flooding. Credit: Umida Maniyazova When her family relocated to Shahimardan, she found herself part of a small, close-knit community with a high degree of confidence in the vaccine, and a high degree of confidence in the counsel of Tursunova. “When Nilyufar explained to me what diseases the HPV vaccine protects against, I agreed. Of course I wanted my daughter to have that protection. Gulbahor received the vaccine here in Shahimardan.” “I understood that what I had heard before was just talk – there was no scientific evidence behind those claims,” she added. “I realised that I had been wrong.” A relationship of trust In a remote community like Shahimardan, the relationship between the health system and families can be especially important. The clinic serves a relatively small population. Parents return to the same health workers with questions, concerns and sometimes information they have heard from neighbours or relatives. The clinic is equipped with the computer equipment and solar panels. Credit: Umida Maniyazova It helps that the local community is proud of their health centre’s competence and reliability. When mountain storms knock the village’s power out, the clinic’s lights – and crucially, its vaccine fridge – stay on. A solar energy system makes sure of that. According to Tursunova, even some clinics in Uzbekistan’s capital cannot boast such a system. Tursunova, meantime, is quite as dependable. She has worked with the local children for eight years in steady, dependable service of a simple goal: parents should not leave the clinic having simply followed an instruction. They should leave understanding why they made that choice for their child. “When a mother understands what the vaccine protects her child from, she no longer needs to be persuaded. She makes the decision herself.” Original article This article was originally published on VaccinesWork Related Articles By addressing cervical cancer prevention and expanding efforts to tackle breast cancer, Uzbekistan is setting an example for public health strategies in Central Asia. content: TODAY’S PAPER | October 17, 2026 | EPAPER ☰ Home Latest Pakistan Business World Sports Opinion Life & Style T-Magazine Blogs Tech Cartoon Home Khyber Pakhtunkhwa HPV drive set to confront endemic vaccine hesitancy As authorities prepare their first campaign to vaccinate girls aged 9 to 14 against cervical cancer, quiet concerns ov Wisal Yousafzai October 12, 2026 3 min read facebook twitter whatsup linkded email HPV drive set to confront endemic vaccine hesitancy PESHAWAR: As Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa (K-P) prepares to launch its first province-wide vaccination campaign against cervical cancer, health authorities face a challenge that goes beyond arranging doses and vaccination teams - convincing parents to have their daughters vaccinated. Cervical cancer is primarily caused by persistent infection with the human papillomavirus (HPV), a virus transmitted through sexual contact. Globally, the disease claims more than 350,000 lives annually, while in Pakistan, more than 5,000 new cases and over 3,000 deaths are estimated each year, making vaccination and early detection crucial. A year after its launch in Punjab and Sindh, the HPV vaccination campaign is now set to reach K-P, where the Health Department plans to vaccinate around 2.9 million girls aged nine to 14 - including 1.6 million school-going and 1.3 million out-of-school girls - between November 2 and November 14. However, health officials and experts acknowledge that reaching every eligible girl will require more than vaccination teams and vaccine doses. Winning the confidence of parents and communities, addressing misinformation and overcoming vaccine hesitancy will be critical to the success of the campaign. This is particularly pertinent in K-P where vaccine hesitancy has assumed an endemic status among the local population given the controversial history of the polio campaign and its links to CIA missions. Even today, K-P continues to record a significant number of refusals during polio campaigns, while vaccination workers have also faced security threats in several areas. Despite these concerns, not all parents are hesitant about the campaign. While some remain wary of the vaccine's safety and possible reactions, others, particularly those who have witnessed the devastating effects of cervical cancer, see vaccination as an important safeguard for their daughters. Bashir Khan, who lost his wife to cervical cancer, said he intended to have both his daughters vaccinated. "Losing my wife has made me particularly conscious of the importance of prevention. Parents should understand the importance of protecting their children from a disease that can have devastating consequences," urged Khan. Conversely, Shamaila Bibi, another parent, was concerned about whether vaccination teams would be properly trained and whether the vaccine could cause reactions among girls. "The problem here is that people often become suspicious even about something positive. If, God forbid, something happens to a girl after vaccination, no parent would want to vaccinate their daughter," she said. Health experts say such concerns need to be addressed through direct communication rather than allowing rumours to fill the information gap. Dr Bawar Shah, president of the Pakistan Paediatric Association's Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa chapter, told The Express Tribune that the HPV vaccine was safe and had been administered in countries around the world. "Cervical cancer is increasing rapidly in Pakistan and vaccination offers an important means of preventing the disease. If parents have any questions or concerns, they should discuss them with the Health Department's vaccination teams and seek clarification," said Dr Shah. Asad Zia, Assistant Director of the Expanded Programme on Immunization (EPI) and in-charge of the Social and Behavior Change (SBC) Cell at the Directorate General Health Services (DGHS) K-P, said awareness campaigns were being conducted in schools, mosques and communities to educate parents about cervical cancer and the HPV vaccine. Zia claimed health teams were also visiting areas where people had concerns about the campaign. In a recent visit to remote Kurram district, officials met religious scholars, community leaders and residents to address their questions and misconceptions about the vaccine. News Newsroom FactCheck Photos Press Releases About Support Us Contact Us FAQ Legal and Privacy Terms Of Use Follow us Facebook Apple News Instagram AAP FactCheck Latest FactChecks Resources How We Work Who We Are Contact Submit A Claim Share Facebook X (Twitter) Copy Link Download Follow Facebook Apple News Instagram Share Facebook x Copy Link Download HPV vaccine rollout in PNG sparks misinformation online Kate Atkinson October 15, 2026 African countries are not abandoning HPV immunisation programs, despite false claims online. Image by EPA PHOTO WHAT WAS CLAIMED African countries are removing an HPV vaccine currently being tested on girls in Papua New Guinea. OUR VERDICT False. The vaccine used in PNG is not new and most African countries have introduced HPV vaccination programs. AAP FactCheck - False claims about the HPV vaccine are circulating online after the Papua New Guinea government launched a national immunisation program to tackle cervical cancer. Among the falsehoods is that PNG is being used as a testing ground for the human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccine while African countries are withdrawing it from use. But the HPV vaccine used in PNG is not new and the number of African countries with HPV immunisation programs has increased in recent years, not decreased. No African countries have discontinued using the vaccine, which is given to young people to protect them against sexually transmitted infections that can cause several types of cancer, including cervical cancer. The claim appeared on social media after the PNG government announced1 2in September that it was embarking on an HPV immunisation program to vaccinate around 60,000 eligible girls aged between nine and 14. "Say No to HPV Vaccine," a September 8 Facebook post3 reads. "We have no proper labs here in PNG to test them. This is one of the "Depopulation Methods" targeted to remove the black population. "All African countries are doing away with this vaccines [sic]. They use PNG as a drug testing zone." False claims about the HPV vaccine spread online after a PNG immunisation program was announced. (Facebook/AAP) The rollout is being led by the National Department of Health in collaboration with the Australian government, UNICEF, the World Health Organization (WHO), Gavi and community groups, according to a joint press release4. A spokesperson for Gavi5, an international organisation that supports immunisation programs in low-income countries, said the Gardasil vaccine used in PNG was developed by pharmaceutical firm Merck. Gardasil was co-developed by Australian researchers and first approved for use in Australia in 20066. "The vaccine has been approved by multiple regulatory authorities and prequalified by the World Health Organization, and has been used in immunisation programmes around the world for many years," the Gavi spokesperson told AAP FactCheck. A spokesperson for UNICEF said HPV vaccines have been used in the Pacific region since 2008, in both Fiji and the Solomon Islands. Health authorities in PNG's Western Highlands Province also began a local immunisation program in 20247, and almost 29,000 girls in the region have been vaccinated, the spokesperson said. The claim that all African countries are abandoning the vaccine is also false. Dr Nosheen Safdar, from the WHO's Regional Office for Africa, said the opposite is happening. "The claim that African countries are abandoning HPV vaccination is false," Dr Safdar told AAP FactCheck. "Thirty-six countries in the WHO African Region now vaccinate girls against HPV, three times as many as in 2019, and more are preparing to join them. Professor Ian Frazer's research in Australia led to the development of the Gardasil vaccine. (Mick Tsikas/AAP PHOTOS8) "Women in Africa face some of the highest cervical cancer death rates in the world, and the HPV vaccine, used safely around the world for 20 years, is one of the most effective tools we have to prevent it." A WHO spokesperson added that no countries in the region had announced plans to withdraw or stop. The WHO publishes a global map9 showing countries that include the HPV vaccine in national immunisation schedules. As of September 2026, the map shows that 36 of the 47 countries in the WHO African region have introduced the HPV vaccine into their national immunisation programmes. A WHO spokesperson told AAP FactCheck that seven of those introductions - Angola, Benin, Comoros, Ghana, Madagascar, Namibia and Burundi - took place since January 2025. The WHO African Region covers 47 of Africa's 54 countries, the spokesperson said. The other seven countries - Djibouti, Egypt, Libya, Morocco, Somalia, Sudan and Tunisia - fall under WHO's Eastern Mediterranean region. The HPV vaccine is included in the immunisation programs of four of the WHO's Eastern Mediterranean nations, with Somalia, Sudan and Egypt being the exceptions, the HPV immunisation map shows. content_title: Groups propose legislation allowing West Virginia dentists, hygienists to administer HPV vaccine
content: Dentist checking patient's teeth. (Photo by Tunvarat Pruksachat/Getty Images) West Virginia's HPV vaccination rates lag below the national average. The state has some of the highest rates for cancers associated with the virus. Some oral health care providers in the state say there's a promising way for West Virginia to address both problems, but it's going to require lawmakers to approve changes to state code. The West Virginia Oral Health Coalition and other organizations want the state Legislature to pass legislation allowing dentists and dental hygienists to administer the HPV vaccine. "(Dental providers are a) ready, educated workforce that can increase access to care around cancer prevention," said Gina Sharps, executive director of the West Virginia Oral Health Coalition. "By recognizing and authorizing dentists and dental hygienists with local anesthetic permits to administer that, then we're just casting a wider net when we look at cancer prevention." The push follows a pilot project by Community Care of West Virginia and Mountains of Hope, the state cancer coalition . The project enlisted dental hygienist Lauren French to talk to her patients in a rural West Virginia county about HPV and the HPV vaccination. HPV can cause oral cancers, among others. French is the only dental hygienist at Community Dental Care of Green Bank, the only dental clinic in Pocahontas County. The clinic sits directly across from the National Radio Astronomy Observatory and near the Monongahela National Forest, so there's no cell service for miles. "It's a pretty cool place to be, but dental care is sparse here... We stay pretty busy. We stay booked out," she said. In the first six months of the project , 34 age-eligible unvaccinated patients were educated about the HPV vaccine. Of them, 10 patients agreed to be vaccinated. But notably, none of those people actually went and got the vaccine, French said. Referring patients even to a nearby medical clinic presented a hurdle for parents, even though they said they were willing to have their children be vaccinated, she said. "(The medical clinic) is just right down the road, but it's one of those things where some people come over for their cleaning. It's scheduled for an hour. They're just taking their lunch break to come do this," French said. "Or they're the last patient of the day, so they're coming after work. They don't have the availability to go right over to the health clinic at that moment." One conclusion from the pilot project was that more kids could be vaccinated for HPV if dental hygienists and dentists were able to administer the HPV vaccine themselves instead of referring people to a medical provider, French said. French said talking about the HPV vaccine fits in nicely with the oral cancer screening they already do with patients. Oral cancer is one of the biggest concerns patients ask about, she said. "It actually is a lot easier to bring up with patients than you might think," French said. "During every routine cleaning, there's an exam... And we're telling the patient, 'We're doing an oral cancer screening just to make sure there's no lumps, bumps, or anything that's suspicious in your mouth.'" And especially with children, there's no need to mention that HPV is a sexually transmitted infection, she said. "The way that I go about it is I don't have to bring up sex at all." she said. "It's just, 'This is a virus that most people come into contact with.' We want them to get vaccinated before they come into contact with this virus. That's why we suggest age 9 to 16 max, getting them fully vaccinated, and that potentially prevents them from getting oropharyngeal cancer or vaginal and penile cancers." French said that about half of her patients were hesitant to get any vaccines, HPV or otherwise. HPV is one of the most common sexually transmitted infections in the United States. Nearly all people are infected with the virus within months or years of becoming sexually active, according to the state Department of Health. In most cases, there are no symptoms and the body clears itself of the infection. In some cases, though, high-risk cases can lead to cervical, vaginal, anal, oropharyngeal, vulvar and penile cancers. The U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention recommends HPV vaccination for pre-teens ages 11 and 12 — before they come in contact with the virus. The vaccine is not part of those required for school attendance in West Virginia. Some people can also catch up on the vaccine later in life if they haven't completed the series at the recommended age. According to the CDC, only about 57% of 13 to 16 year olds in West Virginia were up to date on their HPV vaccine in 2025, compared to 63% in the United States a whole. A CDC report last month found HPV vaccination coverage in rural areas is lower than that of urban areas. West Virginia's HPV vaccination rates have increased in recent years. Lindsay Barr, program manager for the West Virginia Immunization Network, said the difference between the state and national vaccination coverage emphasizes the importance of educating parents and caregivers about the role of the vaccine in preventing cancer. "HPV vaccination is cancer prevention," Barr said. "It not only prevents cervical cancer, but other HPV-associated cancers like oropharyngeal cancer, anal cancer, vaginal, vulva and penile cancers as well. So we think that that lack of knowledge and the confusion among parents plays a big factor in it. So we do a lot to overcome those gaps." Barr said the Immunization Network's survey of parents and caregivers showed that West Virginia parents have a vague understanding of what the HPV vaccine does and little understanding of the negative health outcomes associated with HPV infection. Most parents were only aware that the virus leads to cervical cancer, leading them to believe the vaccine is only recommended for girls, she said. The HPV vaccination recommendation was expanded to include boys in 2009. In West Virginia between 2015 and 2019, HPV accounted for the majority of cervical, vulvar, anal, oropharynx and vaginal cancers in women and the majority of oropharynx cancers in men, according to the West Virginia Department of Health. The vaccine prevents new infections of HPV but does not treat existing ones, Barr said, which is why it's important for people to get vaccinated at young ages and why some medical associations recommend vaccination start at age 9, she said. The HPV Dental Integration Pilot Project has expanded to include Bridge Valley Community and Technical College and the Monongalia County Health Department in Morgantown. West Virginia would not be the first to allow dental professionals to administer the HPV vaccine. Kentucky, Indiana, Louisiana, Massachusetts, Mississippi, New Jersey and Oregon have all passed legislation allowing dental providers to administer the vaccine, according to the Oral Health Coalition. Sharps, with the Oral Health Coalition, said she's drafted bills based on laws in other states. She's not yet approached state lawmakers or gotten sponsors for the bill. The 2027 legislative session begins in January. In order for dental workers to administer the vaccine, state code would have to change and the state Board of Dentistry would have to incorporate the new law into its rules. The board supports allowing dentists to administer the vaccine, according to a position statement on its website. French said dentists and dental hygienists are poised to educate their patients on what HPV causes. They see patients every six months and in some cases every three months, which fits in with the recommended timeline for HPV vaccination doses, she said. Dental hygienists can get certified to administer local anesthesia, a procedure that's more complicated than administering a vaccine, she said. "It's a lot more intricate to anesthetize someone for a tooth or for periodontal procedure or something like that than it is to get an intramuscular vaccination," French said. content: Home Radio TV Videos Movies Advertise Ghana Contact Login NEWS SPORTS BUSINESS POLITICS OPINIONS HEALTH AFRICA WORLD ENTERTAINMENT LIFESTYLE SCIENCE TECHNOLOGY NOLLYWOOD MEDIA MEMBERS Archive Health News Family/Parenting Home/Food Health/Fitness Spirituality OnAIR Search Ho Municipality to conduct HPV vaccination exercise for girls aged 9–14 By Evans Attah Akangla Health WED, 14 OCT 2026 The Ghana Health Service, through its Expanded Programme on Immunization (EPI), will conduct a Periodic Intensification of Routine Immunization (PIRI) exercise focused on Human Papillomavirus (HPV) vaccination in the Ho Municipality from October 19 to 23, 2026. The exercise forms part of efforts to increase HPV vaccination coverage and protect eligible girls against cervical cancer and other HPV-related diseases. In a letter dated October 13, 2026, and signed by the Municipal Director of Health Service, Ms Perfect Titiati, the Directorate said the exercise would target girls aged 9 to 14 years across the municipality. The first round of the vaccination exercise will run from Monday, October 19, to Friday, October 23, 2026. As part of the implementation, trained health personnel will visit schools and other public places to administer the vaccine to eligible girls within the target age group. Health teams will also be stationed at health centres to vaccinate girls who are out of school, with the Directorate stressing that the exercise is intended to ensure that no eligible girl is left behind. Discover more Business Directory Listings News NEWS The Health Directorate said the HPV vaccine is safe and will be provided free of charge. It will be administered as an injection, with one dose providing maximum protection against cervical cancer. Girls who receive the vaccine will be issued immunisation cards as proof of vaccination. The Directorate has therefore urged parents and guardians to take advantage of the exercise and ensure that girls aged 9 to 14 years receive the HPV vaccine. Ms Titiati also appealed to stakeholders in the municipality to help disseminate information about the exercise to the public to ensure a successful vaccination campaign. She expressed confidence in the continued cooperation and support of stakeholders in the municipality. content: Watch Now Menu U.S. News Politics Health World News Investigations Shows Watch Now Watch Now Close × Live Watch Alerts Search site Go Watch Live News Business Crime Education Entertainment Good News Health Scripps News Life Politics Science and Tech Sports U.S. News Weather World News Shows TV Schedule Morning Rush The National Report On the Scene Happening Now in America Today as it Happened Scripps News Weekend In The Shadows with Jason Bellini The Week as it Happened Scripps News Showcase More Shows Documentaries Next Level Bellingcat All Docs Investigations Scripps News Investigates Poisoned: Fentanyl's Child Victims Hope Denied Vacation Rentals: At Your Own Risk Maine Shooting Ukraine's Women Warriors More Investigations Latest Videos About Scripps News News Team Viewer Hotline Download Our App Follow Us Facebook Instagram X TikTok YouTube Threads LinkedIn Newsletter Manage Emails Apps Careers Search scrippsnews scrippsnews scripps-news scrippsnews @scrippsnews Health Bird Flu Medicine Mental Health Recalls More + Quick Links + Health Bird Flu Medicine Mental Health Recalls Health Actions Facebook Tweet Email Millions of cancer cases may be prevented by fighting infections Prev Next Photo by: CI Photos/Shutterstock Gene Therapy for Cancer Treatment Concept Cancer therapy with T-cell and pipette By: Kelly Broderick Posted 4:37 PM, Oct 06, 2026 and last updated 4:40 PM, Oct 06, 2026 A new study published in The Lancet Oncology estimates that 2.3 million cancer cases worldwide in 2024 were attributable to infections. That's roughly 1 in every 8 cancer cases. Researchers found that the infections linked to the largest number of cancer cases are ones that can often be prevented, screened for, treated, or managed. 1/1 Skip Ad Continue watchingafter the adVisit Advertiser websiteGO TO PAGE "This recent Lancet data is a profound reminder that a significant portion of our global cancer burden is fundamentally preventable," said David Greenberg, M.D., medical director of hematology oncology at Hackensack Meridian Jersey Shore University Medical Center and a hematologist-oncologist at Ocean University Medical Center. RELATED STORY | Most women know breast cancer risks, yet they're not acting on them "We have historically siloed infectious diseases and oncology, but they are deeply intertwined. By shifting our focus toward aggressive infection control, we can literally vaccinate and treat our way out of millions of future cancer diagnoses." One example is H. pylori, or Helicobacter pylori, a common bacterial infection that can lead to stomach cancer and has also been linked to an increased risk of colorectal cancer. The infection can spread through saliva or contaminated food and water. It is treatable with antibiotics and medications that reduce stomach acid. Researchers estimated that 760,000 cancer cases worldwide were attributable to H. pylori, making it the leading infection-related cause of cancer in the study. Infectious disease specialist Alex Lazo-Vasquez, M.D., added that hepatitis B and hepatitis C infections can go unnoticed for decades before eventually leading to liver cancer. HPV is another major contributor. The virus can cause several cancers, including cervical cancer in women and penile cancer in men. "Fortunately, we have the tools to protect ourselves. Hepatitis B and HPV are vaccine-preventable, and hepatitis C is now curable with a short course of antiviral medication," Lazo-Vasquez said. "Unfortunately, we are still losing lives to cancers that could potentially be prevented because we are not prioritizing early viral screening and vaccination." The Swedish analysis showed having a human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccine before pregnancy is associated with a lower risk of major pregnancy complications including preterm birth. Reporting the findings in the BMJ, the researchers said the greatest reduction in risk was found in women vaccinated at an earlier age. It follows growing evidence indicating that HPV infection, and the methods used to treat cervical lesions caused by HPV, are linked to an increased risk of pregnancy complications, including preterm birth, the researchers said. They looked at data from 624,713 singleton, first-time births among women aged 16-35 years in Sweden between 2006 and 2023, of whom 15% had received the quadrivalent HPV vaccination before pregnancy. Women with at least one adverse pregnancy outcome, including birth before 37 weeks, very preterm birth between 28 to 31 weeks, preterm and/or pre-labour rupture of membranes, delivering a small or severely small baby, stillbirth, or newborn death, were each matched with 10 controls. After accounting for cigarette use, body mass index at first antenatal visit, maternal diagnoses and assisted reproduction, and various socio-economic factors, they found quadrivalent HPV vaccination was associated with lower odds of all adverse pregnancy outcomes looked at, compared with no vaccination. The association with preterm and very preterm birth, spontaneous preterm birth, preterm prelabour rupture of membranes, and delivering a severely small baby were statistically significant, they said. And reduced risk was generally more pronounced among women vaccinated before age 17, the researchers said. ‘Together with previous research showing the safety of human papillomavirus vaccination during pregnancy, our results suggest that human papillomavirus vaccination is not only safe with respect to pregnancy outcomes but may also confer additional benefits by reducing the risk of adverse events. ‘Collectively, this evidence supports the global strategy for human papillomavirus vaccination and its continued implementation in routine immunisation programmes,’ they added. A UK study published in June found women who received an HPV vaccine as young teenagers have virtually zero risk of dying from cervical cancer before the age of 30. Their analysis reported in The Lancet also found that the HPV vaccine has prevented 200 deaths from cervical cancer in England so far. The number of lives saved will grow as vaccinated generations grow older, and more people receive the vaccination, the team from Queen Mary University of London said. Cheryl Castro, Naval Hospital Twentynine Palms chief nursing officer, stands in a patient examination room in the hospital’s Obstetrics and Gynecology Clinic at Naval Hospital Twentynine Palms, California, Oct. 14, 2026. Castro will serve as a midwife for the hospital’s new walk-in cervical cancer screening services, launching Nov. 9, to improve access to preventive healthcare for eligible beneficiaries. (U.S. Navy photo by Christopher Jones, NMRTC/NH Twentynine Palms public affairs officer). see less | View Image Page TWENTYNINE PALMS, CALIFORNIA, UNITED STATES 10.15.2026 Story by Christopher Jones Naval Hospital Twentynine Palms ✔ ✗ Subscribe 4 TWENTYNINE PALMS, Calif. — Naval Hospital Twentynine Palms will begin offering walk-in cervical cancer screening services Nov. 9, 2026, expanding access to preventive healthcare for service members, military families and other eligible beneficiaries. The new service will be available every Monday from 9 a.m. to noon at Clinic B (OB-GYN), allowing patients to receive routine cervical cancer screenings without scheduling an appointment in advance. “Our goal is to make preventive care easier to access and help patients stay current with recommended screenings,” said Cmdr. Stacie Groves, Naval Hospital Twentynine Palms director for medical services. “Cancer can be a frightening diagnosis. Screening for cervical cancer gives patients and clinicians an opportunity to identify concerns earlier.” The walk-in service will provide Pap tests and human papillomavirus (HPV) co-testing when clinically appropriate. Patients can also discuss their screening history, receive education about recommended screening intervals and learn about any necessary follow-up care. Cmdr. Cheryl Castro, Naval Hospital Twentynine Palms chief nursing officer, who will also serve as a midwife during the walk-in hours, said the initiative builds on successful programs she previously implemented at Naval Hospital Bremerton and Naval Medical Center San Diego. Castro said those programs helped address a common challenge in preventive healthcare: patients having to return on another day for routine screening. “Routine cervical cancer screening is important because early cervical changes often cause no symptoms,” Castro said. “A person can feel completely healthy while abnormal cells are developing.” Cervical cancer screening can identify abnormal cells and allow intervention as indicated before they develop into cancer, making routine screening an important part of preventive healthcare even for patients who are not experiencing symptoms. For patients at average risk, commonly used screening guidelines recommend a Pap test every three years for those ages 21 to 29. For patients ages 30 to 65, screening options include a Pap test every three years, primary high-risk HPV testing every five years, or Pap and HPV co-testing every five years. Screening recommendations may differ depending on individual risk factors, medical history, previous results and facility resources. Castro encouraged eligible beneficiaries who are due for screening, uncertain about their screening history or unable to arrange a routine primary care appointment to take advantage of the new service. “If you are due — or unsure whether you are due — for cervical screening, our midwife-led clinic can help,” Castro said. “Midwives provide routine screening, answer questions, review results and coordinate follow-up with other healthcare professionals when needed.” Following screening, patients will receive their results and follow-up recommendations through the MHS GENESIS Patient Portal. The care team will also advise patients when their next screening is due based on their age, screening results, medical history and applicable guidelines. Patients experiencing symptoms or receiving abnormal results may require additional evaluation. Groves said offering walk-in hours helps eliminate barriers that can prevent patients from receiving recommended preventive care. “Walk-in hours offer another way to access screening and reduce the need to arrange a separate appointment in advance,” Groves said. “That flexibility can help patients fit preventive care around work, military duties, family responsibilities and other demands.” The initiative also supports the Defense Health Agency's mission to improve access to high-quality healthcare while maintaining the medical readiness of service members and their families. “By improving access to preventive care, we directly support the health and readiness of women in uniform and indirectly strengthen our readiness by supporting the health of our warfighters' families,” Groves said. “Healthy service members and families sustain a ready force.” Walk-in cervical cancer screening services begin Monday, Nov. 9, and will be available every Monday from 9 a.m. to noon, excluding federal holidays. Patients should check in at the Clinic B front desk upon arrival. Screenings will be provided on a first-come, first-served basis. For additional information, beneficiaries can contact Clinic B directly at 760-830-2227. Navy Medicine Readiness and Training Command Twentynine Palms operates Defense Health Agency military treatment facility Naval Hospital Twentynine Palms, which delivers safe, high-quality healthcare to service members and their families. The command supports the health and readiness of warfighters at Marine Corps Air Ground Combat Center Twentynine Palms, the Marine Corps’ largest live-fire training installation, while readying Navy Medicine personnel to provide expeditionary medical support around the world. content: The Dhagera and Shillai health blocks of Sirmaur district have secured the first and second positions, respectively, in Himachal Pradesh in a special Human Papillomavirus (HPV) vaccination campaign aimed at protecting adolescent girls against cervical cancer. The Shillai block achieved 103 per cent of its target by vaccinating 513 girls against the target of 490. In recognition of its performance, the team received a trophy and certificate from senior health officials at Hotel Radisson, Shimla. Those present included Secretary (Health) Ashish Singhmar, National Health Mission (NHM) Managing Director Pradeep Thakur and Director of Health Services Dr Gopal Berry. Block Medical Officer (BMO), Shillai, Dr Ajay Deol said the achievement was the result of coordinated efforts by Community Health Officers (CHOs), health workers and supervisors, who worked diligently to ensure that eligible girls received the vaccine. The HPV vaccine protects against infections caused by the Human Papillomavirus, certain types of which can cause cervical cancer. The special campaign was launched by the Government of India and the NHM, Himachal Pradesh, to strengthen preventive healthcare and protect adolescent girls against the disease through timely immunisation. Congratulating the health teams, Chief Medical Officer (CMO), Sirmaur, Dr Rakesh Pratap said, “This achievement reflects the dedication of our frontline health workers and their commitment to protecting the health of adolescent girls. Such efforts will help strengthen preventive healthcare and encourage wider participation in vaccination campaigns.” The Dhagera health block topped the state by vaccinating 855 girls against its target of 756, achieving 115 per cent coverage. Shillai secured the second position with 103 per cent coverage. Officiating BMO, Dhagera, Dr Chavi Bansal said, “The achievement reflects the tireless efforts of our health teams and their commitment to protecting girls from cervical cancer through timely vaccination.” Dr Deol said the recognition would encourage health staff to continue their efforts to improve vaccination coverage and strengthen preventive healthcare services. The state-level recognition is also aimed at motivating other health blocks to improve their performance in government-led immunisation campaigns

(Photo by Tunvarat Pruksachat/Getty Images) West Virginia’s HPV vaccination rates lag below the national average. The state has some of the highest rates for cancers associated with the virus. Some oral health care providers in the state say there’s a promising way for West Virginia to address both problems, but it’s going to require lawmakers to approve changes to state code. The West Virginia Oral Health Coalition and other organizations want the state Legislature to pass legislation allowing dentists and dental hygienists to administer the HPV vaccine. “(Dental providers are a) ready, educated workforce that can increase access to care around cancer prevention,” said Gina Sharps, executive director of the West Virginia Oral Health Coalition. “By recognizing and authorizing dentists and dental hygienists with local anesthetic permits to administer that, then we’re just casting a wider net when we look at cancer prevention.” Dental hygienist talks to patients about HPV in pilot project Lauren French The push follows a pilot project by Community Care of West Virginia and Mountains of Hope, the state cancer coalition. The project enlisted dental hygienist Lauren French to talk to her patients in a rural West Virginia county about HPV and the HPV vaccination. HPV can cause oral cancers, among others. French is the only dental hygienist at Community Dental Care of Green Bank, the only dental clinic in Pocahontas County. The clinic sits directly across from the National Radio Astronomy Observatory and near the Monongahela National Forest, so there’s no cell service for miles. “It’s a pretty cool place to be, but dental care is sparse here... We stay pretty busy. We stay booked out,” she said. In the first six months of the project, 34 age-eligible unvaccinated patients were educated about the HPV vaccine. Of them, 10 patients agreed to be vaccinated. But notably, none of those people actually went and got the vaccine, French said. Referring patients even to a nearby medical clinic presented a hurdle for parents, even though they said they were willing to have their children be vaccinated, she said. “(The medical clinic) is just right down the road, but it’s one of those things where some people come over for their cleaning. It’s scheduled for an hour. They’re just taking their lunch break to come do this,” French said. “Or they’re the last patient of the day, so they’re coming after work. They don’t have the availability to go right over to the health clinic at that moment.” One conclusion from the pilot project was that more kids could be vaccinated for HPV if dental hygienists and dentists were able to administer the HPV vaccine themselves instead of referring people to a medical provider, French said. French said talking about the HPV vaccine fits in nicely with the oral cancer screening they already do with patients. Oral cancer is one of the biggest concerns patients ask about, she said. “It actually is a lot easier to bring up with patients than you might think,” French said. “During every routine cleaning, there’s an exam... And we’re telling the patient, ‘We’re doing an oral cancer screening just to make sure there’s no lumps, bumps, or anything that’s suspicious in your mouth.’” And especially with children, there’s no need to mention that HPV is a sexually transmitted infection, she said. “The way that I go about it is I don’t have to bring up sex at all.” she said. “It’s just, ‘This is a virus that most people come into contact with.’ We want them to get vaccinated before they come into contact with this virus. That’s why we suggest age 9 to 16 max, getting them fully vaccinated, and that potentially prevents them from getting oropharyngeal cancer or vaginal and penile cancers.” French said that about half of her patients were hesitant to get any vaccines, HPV or otherwise. Education important to improving West Virginia’s HPV vaccination rates HPV is one of the most common sexually transmitted infections in the United States. Nearly all people are infected with the virus within months or years of becoming sexually active, according to the state Department of Health. In most cases, there are no symptoms and the body clears itself of the infection. In some cases, though, high-risk cases can lead to cervical, vaginal, anal, oropharyngeal, vulvar and penile cancers. The U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention recommends HPV vaccination for pre-teens ages 11 and 12 — before they come in contact with the virus. The vaccine is not part of those required for school attendance in West Virginia. Some people can also catch up on the vaccine later in life if they haven’t completed the series at the recommended age. According to the CDC, only about 57% of 13 to 16 year olds in West Virginia were up to date on their HPV vaccine in 2025, compared to 63% in the United States a whole. A CDC report last month found HPV vaccination coverage in rural areas is lower than that of urban areas. West Virginia’s HPV vaccination rates have increased in recent years. Lindsay Barr, program manager for the West Virginia Immunization Network, said the difference between the state and national vaccination coverage emphasizes the importance of educating parents and caregivers about the role of the vaccine in preventing cancer. “HPV vaccination is cancer prevention,” Barr said. “It not only prevents cervical cancer, but other HPV-associated cancers like oropharyngeal cancer, anal cancer, vaginal, vulva and penile cancers as well. So we think that that lack of knowledge and the confusion among parents plays a big factor in it. So we do a lot to overcome those gaps.” Barr said the Immunization Network’s survey of parents and caregivers showed that West Virginia parents have a vague understanding of what the HPV vaccine does and little understanding of the negative health outcomes associated with HPV infection. Most parents were only aware that the virus leads to cervical cancer, leading them to believe the vaccine is only recommended for girls, she said. The HPV vaccination recommendation was expanded to include boys in 2009. In West Virginia between 2015 and 2019, HPV accounted for the majority of cervical, vulvar, anal, oropharynx and vaginal cancers in women and the majority of oropharynx cancers in men, according to the West Virginia Department of Health. The vaccine prevents new infections of HPV but does not treat existing ones, Barr said, which is why it’s important for people to get vaccinated at young ages and why some medical associations recommend vaccination start at age 9, she said. Dental professionals in other states administer vaccine The HPV Dental Integration Pilot Project has expanded to include Bridge Valley Community and Technical College and the Monongalia County Health Department in Morgantown. West Virginia would not be the first to allow dental professionals to administer the HPV vaccine. Kentucky, Indiana, Louisiana, Massachusetts, Mississippi, New Jersey and Oregon have all passed legislation allowing dental providers to administer the vaccine, according to the Oral Health Coalition. Sharps, with the Oral Health Coalition, said she’s drafted bills based on laws in other states. She’s not yet approached state lawmakers or gotten sponsors for the bill. The 2027 legislative session begins in January. In order for dental workers to administer the vaccine, state code would have to change and the state Board of Dentistry would have to incorporate the new law into its rules. The board supports allowing dentists to administer the vaccine, according to a position statement on its website. French said dentists and dental hygienists are poised to educate their patients on what HPV causes. They see patients every six months and in some cases every three months, which fits in with the recommended timeline for HPV vaccination doses, she said. Dental hygienists can get certified to administer local anesthesia, a procedure that’s more complicated than administering a vaccine, she said. “It’s a lot more intricate to anesthetize someone for a tooth or for periodontal procedure or something like that than it is to get an intramuscular vaccination,” French said. 1 X Republish Post Groups propose legislation allowing West Virginia dentists, hygienists to administer HPV vaccine by Lori Kersey, West Virginia Watch October 16, 2026

Biénne Huisman unpacks the details in part 3 of a Daily Maverick and Spotlight special series on cancer in South Africa. By Biénne Huisman 12 Oct 2026 Illustrative image: Torn paper edges. (Source: texturefabrik.com) | The Pfukani Mobile Clinic. (Photo: Biénne Huisman – stylised with Google Gemini Flash Image 2.5) | Schoolbag. (Photo: iStock) | Stopwatch. (Photo: iStock) South Africa's cancer story On 1 October, a jubilant mood reigned at the unveiling of the new Pfukani Mobile Clinic in Bushbuckridge, Mpumalanga, with cancer advocates, local residents, health workers and traditional leaders crammed into a community hall. Obstetrician gynaecologists Dr Vincent Shongwe and Dr Martin Namane, who will staff the bright pink-emblazoned truck, were also present. Among other services, Shongwe and Namane will perform pioneering hour-turnaround tests to screen for the cervical cancer-causing human papillomavirus (HPV). Should they pick up a high-risk HPV strain, particularly 16 and 18, they can immediately inspect a patient’s cervix with same-day treatment available for precancerous cervical lesions. On the shoulders of a giant cervical cancer-fighting legacy Inside the mobile clinic, the tests will be done on a GeneXpert machine (primarily used for tuberculosis screening). The late Professor Lynette Denny helped develop and validate the HPV test for the GeneXpert platform in Khayelitsha, Cape Town, about a decade ago. The late Professor Lynette Denny, director of the University of Cape Town’s Gynaecological Cancer Research Centre. (Photo: Nasief Manie / Spotlight) It was Denny’s dream for the hyper-efficient HPV “test and treat” technology to be widely rolled out across South Africa. While this ambition is still in the making (the Department of Health’s 2026 framework for eliminating cervical cancer lists “single-visit test and treat” technology under “future interventions”), the Pfukani Mobile Clinic is a step in the direction Denny was advocating for . The R2-million facility is a public-private partnership between the Mpumalanga Department of Health and healthcare and finances group, Discovery. The Pfukani Mobile Clinic is a purpose-built, solar-powered medical unit that brings breast and cervical health services directly to rural communities in Bushbuckridge. (Photo: Supplied / Spotlight) Shongwe tells Spotlight and Daily Maverick that he was born at Mabuleng Hospital, 2km down the road. “I like to give back, I know what a big problem cervical cancer is in this region,” he says. “I have had someone in my family who died from cervical cancer. And my mom had a malignant lesion but she was treated, and she’s fine. This influenced my decision to become a gynaecologist, but it was my passion even before.” With cervical cancer every day matters With cervical cancer every day matters, says Shongwe, “getting the procedure done as soon as possible is best”. He is referring to thermal ablation, when controlled heat is used to destroy abnormal, precancerous cells on the surface of the cervix; or “large loop excisions of the transformation zone”, where a thin wire loop is used to cut away a small piece of the cervix containing precancerous cells. Discussing the impact of the rapid-screening tests, he says regular HPV test results from a state laboratory could take up to 12 weeks. “We lose some patients,” he says. “ They don’t come back for the results. Even if they do, then it can take up to two to three months for their procedure [thermal ablation or large loop excisions] because of bottlenecks. So this quick test [and same-day treatment with these procedures] will really, really make a difference .” Obstetrician gynaecologists Dr Martin Namane (left) and Dr Vincent Shongwe will staff the mobile clinic. (Photo: Biénne Huisman / Spotlight) Inside the 2m-by-4m clinic’s separate cubicle for clinical examinations, Namane points out their treatment bed and equipment. He explains that HPV testing is different to conventional “pap smears” in that it requires a shallow vaginal swab instead of a deep scraping of the cervix. This means women can swab themselves (“ self sampling ”) should they choose to, he says. A public-private partnership Later, cutting a pink ribbon to loud cheers, provincial health MEC Sasekani Manzini officially opens the mobile clinic, which will rotate around the area and treat about 20 patients a day. Addressing the crowd, she says: “We are grateful for this meaningful gesture... public-private partnerships are crucial in accelerating service delivery and ensuring that no one is left behind.” Manzini encourages women across Mpumalanga to embrace Cheka Impilo (“check your health”) and to prioritise regular screenings – even without symptoms – because early detection saves lives, she says. Traditional healers and cancer Meanwhile, the nonprofit Breast Health Foundation, the driving force behind the mobile clinic, has sought collaboration with traditional healers, providing them with training in cancer awareness. Members of Lesaka La Di Ngaka, the traditional healers collective, Chantel Mokoena and Emily Morweda, inside the Maviljan community hall in Bushbuckridge. (Photo: Biénne Huisman / Spotlight) Speaking at the launch event inside the Maviljan community hall, Chantel Mokoena, a sangoma affiliated to traditional health collective Lesaka La Di Ngaka, says she supports the mobile clinic. “I’m very happy about it,” she says. “With cervical cancer, many people don’t even disclose it. As traditional healers, we want the same things as doctors and nurses, we want people who are healthy.” Read more Two SA women, two very different diagnosis and treatment journeys September 27, 2026 In the area, historically tensions have simmered between nurses and traditional healers. “Sometimes when we refer patients to clinics, sometimes those nurses don’t take us seriously,” Mokoena says. “That’s the problem for us, these doctors and nurses need to treat us like colleagues.” The national picture In Johannesburg, Spotlight and Daily Maverick meet Dr Nonhlanhla Ndlovu, the deputy director-general for HIV, Aids, TB and maternal-child health at the National Department of Health. Ndlovu reiterates that from 2024 HPV screening was introduced in public healthcare as an alternative to pap smears (in alignment with World Health Organization recommendations) since HPV screening detects infection before cellular abnormalities develop, allowing for earlier intervention. She says that, among 928,811 South African women screened for HPV in the public sector in 2025, high-risk HPV strains were detected in 322,611 cases. She is visibly excited about self sampling and rapid HPV tests, saying these are “on the horizon”, but that currently the department cannot allocate budget for a nationwide roll-out. It’s personal For Ndlovu, too, cervical cancer is personal. She says she lost an aunt, who was like an elder sister to her, to stage 3 cervical cancer. Another woman close to her family was diagnosed with stage 3 cervical cancer, despite having had pap smears. The problem is, Ndlovu says, that this family friend never even saw her pap smear results. The woman had chemotherapy and radiotherapy at Grey’s Hospital in Pietermaritzburg and now lives with Ndlovu in Pretoria. “For me, therefore it said the system is broken,” Ndlovu says. Wanting to help work towards a solution partially motivated her last year to assume her present position at the Department of Health. According to a number of sources, cervical cancer is the second-most-common cancer in women in South Africa behind breast cancer. It is also the cancer that claims the second-most lives in the country, again behind breast cancer. Read more Rising tide of cancer diagnosis rates — inside the science, risk factors, human toll October 5, 2026 I n South Africa in 2024, 5,165 women died of cervical cancer, according to the International Agency for Research on Cancer. Ndlovu insists the tragedy of this figure is that these deaths are largely preventable through early detection. Or HPV vaccines. South Africa’s incredible HPV vaccine programme South Africa launched its HPV vaccination programme in 2014 – a collaboration between the departments of Health and Basic Education – which today extends to include girls in public, private and independent schools, with about 3.6 million vaccinated . Health experts agree that the programme is a massive “win”. Dr Nonhlanhla Ndlovu is deputy director-general for HIV, Aids, TB and sexually transmitted infections at the Department of Health. (Photo: Felix Dlangamandla / Daily Maverick) Dr Martin Namane points out their treatment bed and equipment, including a yellow brush for taking swabs. (Photo: Biénne Huisman / Spotlight) Since cervical cancer typically develops quite slowly, it is still too early to see the impact of the HPV vaccination programme in South Africa’s cervical cancer statistics. But there is already good evidence that HPV rates are down. A landmark study on the matter found that HPV rates were 83% lower among a group of vaccine-eligible 17- and 18-year-old girls than it was in an earlier group of 17- and 18-year-old girls who were not eligible. Eligibility is stressed here since not all girls in the eligible group would have been vaccinated. Presenting during a webinar on cervical cancer elimination, co-hosted by the Department of Health on 8 October, obstetrician gynaecologist Professor Helen Rees of the University of the Witwatersrand put South Africa’s current HPV vaccination coverage among the target group at 78%. Commenting on herd immunity (indirect protection from an infectious disease when a large percentage of a population becomes immune), Ndlovu says: “The World Health Organization says if we reach 90% [coverage in the target group, in South Africa girls aged 9 to 15], we will reach herd immunity.” During the same webinar, gynaecological oncologist Professor Hennie Botha of Stellenbosch University described South Africa’s HPV vaccine programme as “a major win”. advertisement Don’t want to see this? Remove ads “The vaccine has proved very efficient and cost effective,” he said. “We’ve made the best choice for South Africa by introducing HPV vaccines into schools.” To illustrate further anticipated success, Botha noted the UK’s national HPV vaccination programme, introduced in 2008. “You can see in a place like the United Kingdom, where they’ve been giving the vaccine now for almost two decades... for the first time now, there’s zero cervical cancers in very young women in England, women who were vaccinated. So that is excellent news. Vaccination will work,” he said. Vaccinating boys? He added that the programme ought to be expanded further into private schools – where parents have proved more hesitant to sign consent forms for their daughters to receive the HPV jab – and that officials need to consider vaccinating boys. Speaking to Spotlight and Daily Maverick, Ndlovu concurs: “If you really wanted to go all the way in terms of prevention of HPV, you would have to vaccinate both boys and girls. But we can’t at the moment from a cost perspective,” she says. Research has shown that HPV vaccination reduces the risk of anal cancer in boys and men. Convening the webinar discussion, Thembi Zulu, deputy director of women’s health at the Department of Health, said: “And as parents it is vital that we sign those consent forms, and that we explain to other parents why it is important for their children to be vaccinated, how it prevents their children from having a deadly disease decades later.” During the webinar, Grade 10 pupil Manala Makua offered a sobering perspective, that teenagers have a right to know what is being administered to them. “Among people I know, I think the general conversation about HPV is nonexistent,” she told the 3,000 webinar attendees. “When I first got the vaccine, I did not really understand what it was for. Many of us have heard about the vaccine but we do not understand what it does to our bodies. Talk to us. Not just about us.” ‘I wish they could see what I face’ Meanwhile, in Bushbuckridge, as fog rolls over the Mpumalanga escarpment, Shongwe says: “ I’m just happy with government for starting this HPV vaccination programme. It’s a very, very important initiative. I understand though that people are scared of vaccinating. I wish they could see what I face in the hospital, seeing people dying from a cancer that can be detected early, that can be cured. I mean, seeing what I see as a doctor, it’s really upsetting.” advertisement Don’t want to see this? Remove ads At the Pfukani Mobile Clinic, Shongwe certainly serves at the coalface of South Africa’s fight to prevent and better detect cervical cancer. “By integrating this unit into our provincial referral system, we ensure that every woman screened receives seamless, dignified care,” MEC Manzini says. “This strengthens our commitment to reaching communities where distance, cost and infrastructure have long limited access to early detection and treatment.” DM This is the third of six articles in the series. Part 1 told the stories of two women who got breast cancer. Part 2 zoomed in on the numbers, and asked whether cancer cases are really going up in South Africa. 1688·工厂直供 360AI・实用工具 一场宫颈癌前病变,可能发生在一个女人最忙碌的几年里。她或许刚刚开始事业,正在计划生育,还没来得及认真想过衰老与疾病。体检报告上的几个字,却可能让这些原本按部就班的生活,突然多出一道必须面对的难题。 过去数十年,面对宫颈癌这个女性健康最常见的“杀手”之一,全球科学家想尽办法。他们先后找到了多种宫颈癌筛查手段,甚至研发出预防性疫苗,终于将越来越多的HPV病毒挡在门外。 但对已经感染HPV的女性来说,这个健康“杀手”的面目依然可怖。 目前,面对高级别宫颈癌前病变,医生最主要的手段是切除病变组织。手术可以去除病灶,却不一定能清除持续存在的HPV感染,还可能带来生育健康风险。长期以来,对有生育计划的年轻女性来说,如何既控制疾病又尽可能保留宫颈功能,是一道两难的选择题。 最近,一款治疗性HPV疫苗,或许将为这道世纪难题带来新解法。 5月20日,北京东方略生物医药科技股份有限公司(下称“东方略”)宣布一项震动产业界的关键进展:其研发的全球首款治疗性HPV疫苗VGX-3100,在中国完成的III期临床试验(HPV-303CHN)已达到预设主要疗效终点,疗效显著优于安慰剂组,且安全性良好。 VGX-3100是全球首款治疗性HPV疫苗,它临床III期的阳性结果,是东方略的一小部,却是人类与宫颈癌斗争之路的一大步。在这一步背后,是一家中国生物医药企业对治疗性疫苗技术路线持续十年的投入,也是宫颈癌防控体系中一个尚待填补的治疗环节。 一个百亿级蓝海市场即将被撬动。 从预防到治疗 HPV感染十分常见,持续感染部分高危型HPV,可能引起宫颈细胞异常变化,并逐步发展为癌前病变甚至宫颈癌。HPV-16和HPV-18是与宫颈癌发生密切相关的高危型别。 2025年发表于《Journal of Infection》的一项观察性研究,分析了2015年1月至2025年9月间3375万余名接受HPV检测的女性数据。研究显示,检测人群的HPV总体阳性率为21.81%,其中高危型HPV阳性率为17.02%。从时间趋势看,整体阳性率由2015年的7.75%升至2025年的22.48%。 国家癌症中心发布的数据显示,2022年我国宫颈癌新发病例为15.1万例,死亡病例是5.6万例,严重威胁女性身心健康。 2016年,中共中央、国务院印发《“健康中国2030”规划纲要》,将宫颈癌防治工作纳入国家战略。2023年,国家卫生健康委等十部门联合发布《加速消除宫颈癌行动计划(2023—2030年)》,明确2030年宫颈癌及癌前病变患者治疗率达到90%,将宫颈癌防控提升至“健康中国”战略的重要高度。 2020年,WHO正式推出《加速消除宫颈癌全球战略》,明确2030年三大核心目标:15岁女孩HPV疫苗接种率达90%、45岁前女性高质量宫颈癌筛查覆盖率达70%、宫颈癌及癌前病变治疗覆盖率达90%。 至此,宫颈癌成为全球首个承诺消除的癌症,VGX-3100的早日获批与应用,将为实现这一全球战略目标提供助力。 要消除宫颈癌,预防性HPV疫苗与治疗性HPV疫苗,承担着不同的任务。预防性疫苗主要用于预防相关HPV感染,不能用于治疗已经形成的宫颈癌前病变;治疗性疫苗则试图调动人体自身的免疫系统,识别并清除已经感染病毒的异常细胞。 对于已经发生高级别宫颈癌前病变的患者,现行治疗主要包括宫颈环形电切术(LEEP)和宫颈锥切术等。手术能够切除病变组织,但仍存在出血、感染、宫颈狭窄等风险,部分患者还可能面临宫颈机能不全等生育相关问题。与此同时,局部切除并不等于清除了持续感染的HPV,后续仍需按照医嘱接受随访和管理。 尤其对有生育需求的年轻女性而言,如何在有效控制病变的同时,尽可能保护宫颈结构,是治疗选择中需要权衡的问题。 治疗性疫苗的探索,正是希望在现有手术方案之外,提供一种新的药物治疗可能。如果能够在临床研究中证实疗效和安全性,并最终获得监管批准,患者未来的治疗选择有望进一步丰富。 用20年,打磨一款治疗性疫苗 VGX-3100是一款针对HPV-16/18相关疾病开发的治疗性DNA疫苗,其研发思路与传统预防性疫苗有所不同。 传统预防性疫苗主要通过诱导机体产生针对病毒的免疫反应,降低感染风险。VGX-3100则通过智能电脉冲递送系统,激活人体T细胞免疫应答,精准清除被HPV16/18感染的细胞,从而实现同时逆转癌前病变与清除潜伏病毒的双重目标。 这一机制的关键,在于细胞免疫。VGX-3100通过激活人体自身免疫系统,识别并清除已经感染病毒的病变细胞,实现根源干预,真正做到标本兼治。 但DNA疫苗的研发也曾面临一个关键难题:DNA分子进入细胞的效率有限,如何让足够的遗传物质进入目标细胞并诱导有效免疫反应,是影响技术发挥作用的重要因素。 VGX-3100采用肌肉注射配合电脉冲递送系统的给药方式。通过毫秒级电脉冲在细胞膜上形成可逆微孔,可显著提升DNA的细胞导入效率,有效解决DNA疫苗递送的核心瓶颈,是目前该领域已验证的关键使能技术之一。也正因为如此,VGX-3100的研发不仅涉及疫苗本身的设计,还需要解决递送系统、制剂工艺和临床给药等多个环节的问题。 VGX-3100并非一款短期内诞生的产品,从研发之初到现在即将问世,已走过了近20年的荆棘之路。 据公开披露,VGX-3100针对宫颈癌前病变的中国III期关键性注册临床研究采用随机、双盲、安慰剂对照设计,由中国医学科学院肿瘤医院吴令英教授牵头,多家三甲医院共同参与。2026年5月20日,相关公告确认研究达到预设主要疗效终点,安全性方面未发现新的重大风险信号。 其实,VGX-3100的意义,不止于一个宫颈癌前病变适应症。 在药物研发中,一款产品能否成功,决定了其自身的临床和商业价值;而一条技术路线能否在不同疾病中得到验证,则关系到企业未来的研发空间。对东方略而言,围绕VGX-3100积累的DNA药物设计、递送系统和临床开发经验,是其持续布局相关领域的基础。 除宫颈癌前病变外,东方略还在推进VGX-3100针对其他HPV相关疾病的研究。目前,该产品已获得针对肛门癌前病变和阴道癌前病变的II期临床试验许可。未来,VGX-3100有机会覆盖更广泛的HPV相关疾病。 “特别声明:以上作品内容(包括在内的视频、图片或音频)为凤凰网旗下自媒体平台“大风号”用户上传并发布,本平台仅提供信息存储空间服务。 Notice: The content above Home News Iloilo Free HPV vaccines pushed to shield girls in Western Visayas from cervical... News Iloilo Free HPV vaccines pushed to shield girls in Western Visayas from cervical cancer By Neljoy N. Galigao - Wednesday, October 14, 2026 Facebook X Viber Print ILOILO — The Department of Health (DOH) is stepping up efforts to protect young girls in Western Visayas from cervical cancer, urging parents to take advantage of free human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccination before their daughters become vulnerable to the virus responsible for nearly all cases of the potentially deadly disease. It emphasized that girls aged nine to 14 should receive the vaccine early to significantly reduce their risk of developing cervical cancer later in life. The renewed campaign highlights the importance of preventing a disease that remains among the leading causes of cancer deaths among Filipino women, despite being largely preventable through vaccination and regular screening. Health authorities stressed that administering the HPV vaccine before exposure to the virus provides stronger protection against high-risk HPV infections associated with cervical cancer. Discover more See an OB-GYN Find Cancer Care Book a Checkup Under its campaign slogan, “Proteksyon Karon, Paglaum sa Palaabuton,” DOH Region 6 is encouraging parents and guardians to consider vaccination an essential investment in their daughters’ health and future. “Today, Inday is just a grade school learner, but in the future, she could become a doctor, teacher, engineer, artist, or professional,” DOH-6 stated in its advisory. “Whatever her dream may be, let us help her grow up healthy and protected,” it added. The agency underscored that protecting young girls against preventable diseases would allow them to pursue their education, careers and aspirations without the burden of illnesses that could have been prevented. CERVICAL CANCER THREAT Cervical cancer develops when abnormal cells grow uncontrollably in the cervix, the lower portion of the uterus connecting to the vagina. Almost all cases are associated with persistent infections caused by high-risk types of HPV, particularly types 16 and 18, which account for the majority of cervical cancer cases. Although HPV infections are common, certain persistent infections can eventually cause abnormal cellular changes that may develop into cancer if left undetected and untreated. Health officials emphasized that early vaccination, combined with regular cervical cancer screening later in life, provides an effective defense against the disease. “Regular screening and HPV vaccination are among the most crucial steps to prevent cervical cancer,” the agency added. Screening procedures, including Pap smears and visual inspection with acetic acid, help detect abnormal changes in cervical cells before they progress into cancer. FREE VACCINATION AVAILABLE DOH-6 reminded parents that HPV vaccines are available free of charge through government health facilities, including local health centers, rural health units and school-based immunization programs. Discover more Find Vaccines vaccines vaccine Parents and guardians of girls aged nine to 14 are encouraged to coordinate with their nearest barangay health stations or municipal health offices to inquire about vaccination schedules, dosage requirements and available consultation services. The agency stressed that vaccination during the recommended age range is particularly important because the vaccine works best when administered before exposure to HPV. “Approach our local health centers to get vaccinated. Disease prevention begins with sound preparation for tomorrow—for every young girl, for every dream, toward a healthier future,” DOH-6 stressed./PN RELATED ARTICLESMORE FROM AUTHOR Iloilo MASSKARA’S GRAND WEEKEND: Smiles, love take center stage Iloilo Iloilo tightens sugarcane movement to stop pest spread Iloilo Dengue deaths rise in Iloilo despite 16% drop in cases LEAVE A REPLY Cancel reply Please enter your comment!
