BJACH helps patients take the next step By Jean GravesOctober 14, 2026 From left, 1st Lt. Allison Hubner, physical therapist; 1st Lt. Quinne Johnson, occupational therapist; and Taylor Fleter, physical therapy technician, pose during Bayne-Jones Army Community Hospital’s Organizational Day at Alligator Lake, Fort Polk, Louisiana, Sept. 3, 2026. BJACH encourages beneficiaries to discuss recommended cancer screenings with their primary care manager as part of maintaining their health. ... READ MORE From left, Shawna Wilkerson, physician assistant; Anna Pinkelman, licensed clinical social worker; and Crystal Langston, registered nurse, pose during Bayne-Jones Army Community Hospital’s Organizational Day at Alligator Lake, Fort Polk, Louisiana, Sept. 3, 2026. BJACH’s primary care and population health teams help patients identify screening needs and access preventive care. ... READ MORE FORT POLK, La. — Busy schedules, uncertainty and anxiety can keep patients from completing cervical cancer screening. At Bayne-Jones Army Community Hospital, population health and clinical teams work together to help patients understand their screening needs and access care. “Each ‘overdue’ screening has a human story behind it,” said June Lyons, a registered nurse in population health at BJACH. Lyons uses health records and screening data to identify patients who may be due for preventive care. Outreach includes calls, patient portal messages, letters and text messages linking to educational materials through the Defense Health Agency’s Virtual Education Center. “At BJACH, it’s not just about a number or score,” Lyons said. The goal is to understand what stands between patients and care, then help them take the next step. Maj. Briana Thurmond, an obstetrician-gynecologist at BJACH, encourages screening even when patients feel well. Identifying abnormal cervical cells before they become cancerous can allow earlier intervention. Thurmond emphasized that a pelvic examination does not automatically include a Pap test. A pelvic exam may be performed for discomfort, abnormal discharge or other concerns without cervical cancer screening. A Pap test specifically samples cervical cells, while HPV testing checks for human papillomavirus. Providers consider age, medical history and previous results when recommending screening. A Pap test is not automatically needed every year. Patients can ask whether screening is being performed and when their next screening is due. For patients anxious about a sensitive examination, Thurmond explains each step, moves at their pace and respects their control over the process. “If at any point I am told to stop the exam, I will stop immediately,” she said. DHA’s chaperone policy provides another layer of support during sensitive examinations. Staff must offer a chaperone before a sensitive exam, with exceptions for certain emergency situations. Patients can request a chaperone of their preferred sex without explaining why. Staff will make reasonable efforts to accommodate the request and offer rescheduling if the requested chaperone is unavailable. Routine cervical cancer screening can be completed through primary care without a gynecology referral. If results require additional evaluation, the care team explains the findings and coordinates follow-up. Patients screened outside BJACH should share their results with the care team so their military health records can be updated. Lyons encourages patients to ask their primary care team whether they are due for screening. “We are here to walk alongside you on your healthcare journey, not just to perform a procedure,” she said. To discuss screening or arrange an appointment, call 726-780-2175 or contact your care team through the MHS GENESIS Patient Portal. Editor’s note: This is the first in a three-part series highlighting cervical, colorectal and breast cancer screening at BJACH. content_title: Prepregnancy HPV Vaccination Linked to Lower Risk for Adverse Pregnancy Outcomes
content: WEDNESDAY, Oct. 14, 2026 (HealthDay News) -- Quadrivalent human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccination before pregnancy is associated with a lower risk for adverse pregnancy outcomes, including preterm birth, according to a study published online Oct. 7 in The BMJ . Zhongsong Zhang, from Karolinska Institutet in Sweden, and colleagues conducted a nationwide, population-based, matched case-control study to examine the association between quadrivalent HPV vaccination before pregnancy and the subsequent risk for adverse pregnancy outcomes. Data were included for 624,713 singleton births among nulliparous women in Sweden between 2006 and 2023; 14.8 percent had received quadrivalent HPV vaccination before pregnancy. The researchers found that quadrivalent HPV vaccination was associated with lower odds of all included adverse pregnancy outcomes after adjustment for confounders. Significant associations were seen for preterm birth (<37 weeks), very preterm birth (28 to 31 weeks), spontaneous preterm birth, preterm prelabor rupture of membranes, and severe small for gestational age (adjusted odds ratios, 0.95, 0.85, 0.95, 0.93, and 0.92, respectively). Women vaccinated at younger ages generally had a more pronounced risk reduction. "Beyond the established benefits of HPV vaccination in cancer prevention, the demonstrated reductions in adverse pregnancy outcomes associated with vaccination before conception may translate into substantial long-term health and economic benefits," the authors write.
